title: Bridesmaids
logline: Kristen Wiig as a maid of honor whose life is falling apart. Improvised character comedy with set pieces.
overview: Annie's life is a mess. But when she finds out her lifetime best friend is engaged, she simply must serve as Lillian's maid of honor. Though lovelorn and broke, Annie bluffs her way through the expensive and bizarre rituals. With one chance to get it perfect, she’ll show Lillian and her bridesmaids just how far you’ll go for someone you love.

jokes.text: Opening scene of two people having sex, intercut with what sounds like workout instructions — 'Cup my balls.' / 'Okay, yes. All right. I can do that.'
jokes.setup: The scene opens with breathless, intimate-sounding dialogue ('I love your eyes,' 'Oh! There it is') that could be romantic or workout-based, leaving the audience briefly uncertain
jokes.punchline: 'Cup my balls' — delivered mid-scene, confirms this is explicitly sexual and deflates any romantic ambiguity
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection opening — the film earns a solid laugh by being bluntly sexual right out of the gate. Not particularly original (sex-scene openings are a rom-com staple) but the bluntness of 'cup my balls' as the first real laugh is well-timed.

jokes.text: 'Yeah. No, I want to go fast.' / 'You want to go fast? Fast.'
jokes.setup: They've slowed sex down to a tender moment ('slow it down... doesn't that feel good?')
jokes.punchline: Annie immediately reverses, wanting fast — undercutting any semblance of intimacy or compatibility
jokes.explanation: Light laugh — the rhythm joke (slow/fast) works as an escalation of the opening misdirection. It's a small beat that shows the two are out of sync, which is both literally and metaphorically true of Annie and Ted's relationship.

jokes.text: 'I think maybe we are on different rhythms here.'
jokes.setup: The couple keeps going back and forth on fast vs. slow, creating an almost comedically incompatible sexual dynamic
jokes.punchline: Annie's clinical, politely phrased conclusion — 'different rhythms' — is a massive understatement for what is clearly a dysfunctional hookup
jokes.explanation: Annie's polite, diplomatic language in the middle of sex is very 'her' — it shows her character's tendency toward socially appropriate language even in awkward situations. The understatement is the joke. Good economy.

jokes.text: Ted tells Annie she looks beautiful; she deflects; then Ted reveals he thought they had a rule against sleepovers — 'I thought we had a rule against that.' / 'Oh.' / 'I'm kidding. Oh. That was funny. I'm kidding.'
jokes.setup: Ted tells Annie she's beautiful and seems warm — building the false impression he might actually care
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he doesn't want her sleeping over, then has to walk back the cruelty ('I'm kidding') — exposing his complete emotional unavailability AND his social awkwardness about it
jokes.explanation: This is sharp character work. Ted's bumbling attempt to soften his cruelty ('I'm kidding... that was funny... I'm kidding') is painfully real and reveals exactly who he is. The rewatch bonus is for the way this retroactively reframes the whole opening.

jokes.text: Annie's speech: 'I'm not looking for a relationship right now, either... I'm not like other girls... I'm not like, "Be my boyfriend!" Unless you were like, "Yeah!" Then I'd be like, "Maybe."'
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to match Ted's casual 'I don't want a relationship' energy and convince him (and herself) she's chill
jokes.punchline: Her speech immediately collapses — 'Unless you were like, Yeah! Then I'd be like, Maybe' — revealing she absolutely would want to be his girlfriend. The 'I'm not like other girls' line is also self-aware cringe.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The structure is perfect: Annie builds an elaborate case for being low-maintenance and 'not like other girls,' then immediately demolishes it in the same breath. 'Unless you were like yeah then I'd be like maybe' is a brilliant self-betrayal. High character integration — this could only be Annie. Earned, not cheap.

jokes.text: 'Wow, this is so awkward. I really want you to leave, but I don't know how to say it without sounding like a dick.'
jokes.setup: Post-sex awkwardness — Ted and Annie are in a vague no-commitment arrangement
jokes.punchline: Ted says the quiet part loud — his 'solution' to not sounding like a dick is to narrate exactly what he's doing while doing it, which IS being a dick
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the reel. Ted's complete lack of self-awareness — explaining that he doesn't want to sound like a dick by saying something that makes him sound exactly like a dick — is a perfect character joke. The line is quotable, economical, and reveals character in a single breath. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor: sharp, unexpected, perfectly constructed.

jokes.text: Drill-sergeant instructor screaming at park exercisers: 'You're looking like pieces of bacon on a plate. It's disgusting! I smell the fat!'
jokes.setup: Transition to Annie and her best friend Lillian exercising in the park, implying a normal workout scene
jokes.punchline: The instructor is comically deranged — 'I smell the fat' is an absurd, almost supernatural claim that escalates the insult past normal into surreal territory
jokes.explanation: 'I smell the fat' is the best line here — it tips the insult from mean into absurdist and earns the laugh. Solid if unremarkable. The 'bacon on a plate' image is vivid. Character is a one-note archetype, but serves the scene.

jokes.text: Annie and Lillian freeloading the workout class from a distance; instructor spots them: 'Hey! If you want to take this class, you're going to have to pay for it like the rest of these bitches!'
jokes.setup: The two women are watching from the sidelines, apparently getting the workout for free
jokes.punchline: 'Like the rest of these bitches' — the instructor's choice of words for his paying clients is the unexpected escalation that makes this land
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the word 'bitches' — it's the instructor's casual contempt for his own paying customers. Fun but slight.

jokes.text: Annie and Lillian running away from the instructor screaming 'freeloaders!' — visual chase gag with him threatening to come after them
jokes.setup: The instructor has spotted them and is escalating his threats
jokes.punchline: The sheer absurdity of a fitness instructor chasing down two women over a free workout, combined with their panicked running, is a visual payoff
jokes.explanation: Physical payoff to the drill instructor setup. Works but doesn't add much beyond the previous two jokes. The 'you fucking freeloaders' exit line is the peak of this bit.

jokes.text: 'We are out of our minds.' / 'I know.' — Annie and Lillian laughing at themselves after fleeing the instructor
jokes.setup: They've just fled a screaming man over a free workout
jokes.punchline: The cheerful self-awareness — 'we are out of our minds' — lands as a beat of genuine friendship warmth that also punctuates the absurdity
jokes.explanation: More of a tone reset than a joke — it's a small laugh that transitions into exposition. Functional, not special.

jokes.text: Lillian mentions her boyfriend calls her 'dude' a lot as evidence he might be distant; Annie dismisses it: 'That doesn't mean anything. I think everything is fine.'
jokes.setup: Lillian is anxiously listing signs her boyfriend might be pulling away, including being called 'dude'
jokes.punchline: Annie's breezy dismissal of a pretty telling sign is both funny and ironic given her own situation with Ted
jokes.explanation: Light laugh, but gains value on rewatch because we know the 'distance' is because Dougie is secretly planning a proposal — not because he's pulling away. Annie's wrong for the right reasons.

jokes.text: 'Ew! You had sex with him.' / 'We had an adult sleepover.'
jokes.setup: Lillian presses Annie on what she did last night with Ted; Annie reluctantly confirms she saw him
jokes.punchline: Annie's euphemism 'adult sleepover' for sex is a perfect piece of Wiig-ian verbal comedy — prissy, evasive, and oddly charming
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever. 'Adult sleepover' is a perfect euphemism — it's the kind of thing Annie would say, and it works as both a character moment and a callback to the sleepover joke in the previous scene. High quotability, great economy, strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'Ooh. Did you let him sleep over in your mouth?'
jokes.setup: Annie's euphemism 'adult sleepover' — Lillian plays on the word 'sleepover'
jokes.punchline: Lillian's crude follow-up — a graphic oral sex joke delivered with cheerful energy — is unexpected from the apparently sweet best friend
jokes.explanation: Quick, sharp callback that scores because of its economy and unexpectedness. The 'sleep over in your mouth' construction is clever wordplay that escalates the previous joke.

jokes.text: Annie recounting Ted putting it near her face: 'He kept putting it near my face.' / 'They do that, don't they? / Why do they do that? Let us offer. / If we don't offer... / You're supposed to slap it away. / I couldn't.'
jokes.setup: Lillian has asked if Annie let Ted sleep over 'in her mouth'; Annie starts to explain the situation
jokes.punchline: The two women have a fully normalized, clinical discussion about an experience they've apparently both had — the etiquette of 'slapping it away' — which is both vulgar and charmingly matter-of-fact
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from the shared female perspective and the casual, almost procedural tone — 'let us offer,' 'you're supposed to slap it away.' It's funny because it's specific, real, and delivered with zero shame.

jokes.text: 'You don't want to look right at it. No. It's too aggressive. It's like...' [pause] '"Hello."' / 'That's my impression.' / 'Those are the balls? / Yeah. I'm trying to make it round but I can't because I have elbows.'
jokes.setup: The conversation about Ted's behavior in bed has escalated to impressions
jokes.punchline: Annie does a physical impression of a penis — with her arms, trying to make a round shape — and admits the limitation: 'I can't because I have elbows.' The word 'Hello' is delivered as the penis greeting them.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The setup ('too aggressive, it's like...') followed by Annie's physical impression and the word 'Hello' is surreal and perfectly executed. The addition of 'I can't because I have elbows' is a masterful escalation — it's so specific and so absurd. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its unexpectedness and economy.

jokes.text: Lillian tells Annie she 'doesn't need dental work'; Annie: 'I don't need dental work.' / [beat] 'You're right. There is nothing wrong with my teeth.'
jokes.setup: Lillian has mentioned that Ted told Annie she needs dental work (as an example of him being an asshole)
jokes.punchline: Annie's delayed, slightly over-insistent self-reassurance — 'there is nothing wrong with my teeth' — reveals this comment has actually gotten under her skin
jokes.explanation: Small but effective character moment. The beat before 'you're right' tells us Annie is wounded, and 'there is nothing wrong with my teeth' is classic comic over-protestation.

jokes.text: 'He also told you that you need dental work. He's an asshole.'
jokes.setup: Annie defends Ted by saying 'He's honest! He told me that we are what we are and we're just having fun.'
jokes.punchline: Lillian lands a devastating kicker — Ted apparently told Annie she needs dental work, which reframes 'his honesty' as cruelty, not virtue.
jokes.explanation: Superb structure. Annie sets up the defense ('he's honest') and Lillian immediately demonstrates that Ted's 'honesty' extends to deeply hurtful personal criticism. The dental work detail is specific enough to feel like a real memory, and 'He's an asshole' as the deadpan conclusion lands with real force. Highly quotable. The specificity of dental work (not, say, 'your haircut') makes it funnier — it's such an odd, vulnerable thing to criticize.

jokes.text: 'You are so beautiful. / Will you marry me? / Yes.' — Annie and Lillian fake-proposing to each other on a park bench
jokes.setup: The conversation has gone from Ted's cruelty to Lillian reassuring Annie she's beautiful
jokes.punchline: The spontaneous mock proposal between best friends — delivered with complete sincerity and immediately accepted — is both sweet and funny as a commentary on what Annie actually needs vs. what she's getting from Ted
jokes.explanation: Gains a rewatch bonus because Lillian is literally about to get engaged — the mock proposal is an ironic preview. In the moment it's a warm, funny beat. Not a big laugh but charming.

jokes.text: 'Let's see how many times Terry's called me. Oh! Only 15! You know what, Terry? I don't want to pick up your monkey lamps. Sorry!' / 'Monkey lamps?'
jokes.setup: Annie checks her phone, irritated by her boss Terry
jokes.punchline: 'Monkey lamps' — the specificity of this absurd detail (what on earth is a monkey lamp and why does Terry urgently need them?) is the joke. Lillian's incredulous 'Monkey lamps?' mirrors the audience.
jokes.explanation: The random specificity of 'monkey lamps' is perfect absurdist comedy. It's funny because it's so specific that it feels real, while also being surreal enough to get a laugh. '15 calls' escalates the horror of the job. Strong economy.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry. I should have gone down Mason.' / 'Well, I'm the genius that opened a bakery during the recession.'
jokes.setup: They're passing Annie's former bakery, apparently now closed
jokes.punchline: Annie's dry self-deprecation — calling herself 'the genius' who opened a business during an economic crash — is delivered with practiced resignation rather than self-pity, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Good character exposition delivered through self-deprecating irony. 'The genius' construction is a classic understatement move. The resigned tone (not wallowing) keeps it light.

jokes.text: 'They were good cakes, Annie.' / 'Thank you.' / 'Come on. Look away, look away, look away.'
jokes.setup: Lillian tries to console Annie about the failed bakery
jokes.punchline: Lillian's gentle 'look away' — hurrying them past the closed shop as if it's a roadside accident — is a physically comedic beat that's also genuinely touching
jokes.explanation: 'Look away, look away, look away' has an incantatory quality that's funny and sweet. It treats Annie's failed business like a traumatic crime scene, which is the right level of absurd-earnest.

jokes.text: Annie, working at a jewelry store, watches a couple sweetly deciding on an engagement ring and comments: 'That will go away.'
jokes.setup: A newly engaged couple is adorably finishing each other's sentences and making decisions together warmly — Annie is their sales clerk
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat, matter-of-fact 'that will go away' — said directly to the couple about their evident love — is the perfect dark-comedy puncture of the saccharine moment
jokes.explanation: Three words, devastating comedy. 'That will go away' spoken to two happy newlyweds by their jewelry store clerk is an exquisitely dark beat. It characterizes Annie perfectly — she's not bitter enough to leave, but too broken not to say it. Near-perfect economy (9.5), strong character integration. Genuinely exceptional line delivery moment. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: 'You cannot trust anybody, ever. Especially someone you're in a relationship with. 'Cause they're living with you, you don't know who you're sleeping next to. It is scary. I mean, look at him. He may not even be Asian.'
jokes.setup: Following her 'that will go away' quip, Annie continues her unsolicited anti-marriage monologue to the browsing couple
jokes.punchline: 'He may not even be Asian' — a sudden, surreal escalation into racial paranoia that makes no logical sense but is delivered with complete earnestness, suggesting Annie has genuinely spiraled
jokes.explanation: Brilliant escalation. The speech starts with generic paranoia ('you can't trust anyone'), which is funny but expected from Annie, and then goes completely off the rails with 'he may not even be Asian' — a leap of logic so bizarre it's genuinely surprising. The confidence of the delivery is key. This is subversive absurdism at its best.

jokes.text: Annie's boss Don corrects her behavior with the couple: 'You're not telling everyone about your problems and how your boyfriend left you, and maybe marriage will work out.' / 'Show me your "love is eternal" face.'
jokes.setup: Annie has apparently driven away customers; Don tries to coach her
jokes.punchline: Don's matter-of-fact summary of Annie's speech — 'your boyfriend left you and maybe marriage will work out' — is funnier for how accurately it captures Annie's nihilism. 'Show me your love is eternal face' is a great absurd coaching request.
jokes.explanation: Good workplace comedy — the boss having to explain 'show me your love is eternal face' as a job requirement is funny. The blunt recap of Annie's situation is also well-structured.

jokes.text: Annie attempts the 'love is eternal' face — apparently looking like she has cramps: 'No, that's two years, four years tops. That is not eternal.'
jokes.setup: Don has asked Annie to show him her 'love is eternal' face to demonstrate what she should do with customers
jokes.punchline: Don's critique — 'that's two years, four years tops' — implies Annie's attempt at a loving face looks like a timed relationship, not eternity. The face itself is a visual gag.
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed. Don's specific 'two years, four years tops' scores because it's not just 'that looks bad' — it quantifies exactly how limited Annie's optimism is. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: Don calls his co-worker 'Kahlua' and asks her to demonstrate the 'love is eternal' face: 'You don't need a nickname because Kahlua is so delicious. Don't sue me for touching you.'
jokes.setup: Don is demonstrating what a good salesperson looks like vs. Annie
jokes.punchline: 'Don't sue me for touching you' — Don's pre-emptive disclaimer about touching his employee, delivered mid-pep-talk, reveals his chronic HR-adjacent anxiety and is a great absurdist aside
jokes.explanation: Don is a weird, specific character and 'don't sue me for touching you' is a great little moment of his obliviousness. The name 'Kahlua' as a real employee name is also a funny recurring detail.

jokes.text: Don calls over Kahlua: 'Kahlua, can you come over here for a second, please? What's up, Don-Don? You make up the best nicknames. You don't need a nickname because Kahlua is so delicious. Don't sue me for touching you.'
jokes.setup: Don wants to show Annie how to do the 'love is eternal' face properly; he summons his colleague Kahlua.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't sue me for touching you' — after establishing affectionate nicknames and complimenting her name, Don's immediate preemptive HR disclaimer is funny and reveals a character.
jokes.explanation: Don's self-aware HR disclaimer is funny, particularly after the warm nickname exchange. 'Don't sue me for touching you' captures a certain kind of workplace awkwardness — the person who is both overfamiliar AND aware they're being overfamiliar.

jokes.text: Kahlua's 'love is eternal' face causes Don to say: 'That looks like you have menstrual cramps.'
jokes.setup: Don held up Kahlua as the gold standard for the 'love is eternal' face
jokes.punchline: Even the supposedly good employee's face looks like menstrual cramps to Don — undercutting his entire argument about Annie being uniquely bad
jokes.explanation: Good subversion — Don's parade of 'good examples' all fail his own test. The specificity of 'menstrual cramps' is funnier than a generic 'that looks wrong.'

jokes.text: Don reveals to Annie that the only reason she has the job is because her mom is his AA sponsor: 'The whole reason you have got this job, Annie, is because your mom is my sponsor in AA, and I'm doing her a favor.'
jokes.setup: Don has been lecturing Annie about performance; it seems like normal workplace tension
jokes.punchline: Don reveals the entire premise of her employment — casually, as a motivational note — exposing both his social inappropriateness and Annie's rock-bottom situation
jokes.explanation: Dark and efficient. Don's obliviousness in deploying this as a pep talk is the joke — he thinks this is motivating. It deepens Annie's humiliation in a funny, honest way.

jokes.text: 'Oscar, get back to work. You shouldn't be behind the counter.'
jokes.setup: Don is in the middle of lecturing Annie
jokes.punchline: Don mid-speech suddenly has to manage another employee who apparently wanders behind the counter — a background chaos beat that shows the whole store is barely held together
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh — the 'Oscar' interruption adds texture to Don's chaotic management style but isn't a strong joke on its own. Functions as world-building background comedy.

jokes.text: TV in background playing Maury: 'Andrew, you are not the father!' — Don and Annie pause to react
jokes.setup: Don is continuing his lecture; there's a TV on in the jewelry store
jokes.punchline: The Maury Povich paternity reveal playing on the store TV cuts through the scene — Don and Annie both momentarily engage with it ('That's great. Yeah.') before Don remembers himself ('Stop that. Don't do that.')
jokes.explanation: The Maury bit works because both characters involuntarily respond to it, breaking the tension of the lecture. 'That's great. Yeah.' followed by 'Stop that. Don't do that.' is a small but well-executed beat. Familiar reference used with just enough specificity.

jokes.text: Annie's roommate Brynn announces she got a free tattoo from a guy who 'opened up the side of his van'
jokes.setup: Annie comes home; Brynn greets her with apparent excitement
jokes.punchline: The van tattoo — the most dangerous possible tattoo acquisition method — is delivered by Brynn with complete enthusiasm, establishing her as an obliviously chaotic roommate
jokes.explanation: Good character introduction for Brynn — her obliviousness is established immediately. 'He opened the side of his van' as a tattoo parlor is a great absurdist image.

jokes.text: The tattoo is a 'Mexican drinking worm' / 'It's a Native American symbol meaning "wasted"'
jokes.setup: Brynn shows off the free van tattoo
jokes.punchline: The tattoo's meaning — first described as a 'Mexican drinking worm,' then elevated to a 'Native American symbol meaning wasted' — escalates the absurdity. The 'wasted' meaning is the perfect ironic capstone.
jokes.explanation: The escalating explanation of the tattoo — from 'drinking worm' to 'symbol meaning wasted' — is very funny. Brynn's earnestness about the apparent cultural significance of her terrible van tattoo is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Annie's other roommate Gil enters and mentions the tattoo is infected, then matter-of-factly suggests 'stick some frozen peas on there'
jokes.setup: Annie is alarmed by the infected tattoo; Gil is apparently aware of it
jokes.punchline: Gil's completely nonchalant medical advice — 'stick some frozen peas on there' — for what sounds like a serious infection is funny in its inadequacy and casualness
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh. Gil's uselessness is established quickly. The 'frozen peas' advice is a classic underreaction to a problem that probably requires medical attention.

jokes.text: 'Because it's a kind of, like, "needing it today"-type situation.'
jokes.setup: Annie says she's 'getting the money'; Gil pushes back
jokes.punchline: Gil's hilariously passive construction — 'needing it today-type situation' — is the kind of elaborately casual phrasing people use when they don't want to be direct, and it perfectly captures his personality
jokes.explanation: 'Needing it today-type situation' is a nice piece of character-specific verbal comedy — the hedging ('kind of, like') around what is a very simple demand is funny and revealing.

jokes.text: Lillian holds up her hand with the engagement ring: 'What is that? / I got engaged.' — Annie and friend react with physical shock ('I just got hot. My pits are sweating. My stomach hurts.')
jokes.setup: Lillian has shown up at Annie's apartment; Annie and her other roommate are having a wine-and-magazine night
jokes.punchline: Annie's visceral, almost medical reaction to the engagement news — sweating pits, hot flashes, stomach hurt — is a funny, physical escalation of normal excitement into something almost symptomatic
jokes.explanation: Annie's cataloging of her physical symptoms as the engagement news hits — 'pits are sweating, stomach hurts, I'm hot' — is a funny literalization of overwhelming emotion. Good character work.

jokes.text: 'Oh! Look at that. It's my fiancé calling. / Oh, your fiancé.' — Lillian's delight at calling Dougie her 'fiancé' for the first time
jokes.setup: Lillian's phone rings immediately after the engagement revelation
jokes.punchline: Lillian's slightly giddy pleasure at using the word 'fiancé' — and Annie mirroring it back ('oh, your fiancé') with a mixture of affection and mild despair — is a small, real beat
jokes.explanation: Gentle, warm beat. Not a big laugh but a true one — Lillian's pride in the new word is charming and Annie's echo is bittersweet. Functions more as emotional texture than pure comedy.

jokes.text: 'It's Annie. I just told her! Yeah, she's so happy.' / 'No, I'm not!'
jokes.setup: Lillian is on the phone with Dougie, narrating Annie's reaction to the news
jokes.punchline: Annie's reflexive 'No, I'm not!' — immediately correcting Lillian's claim that she's happy — is a funny, honest moment that reveals Annie's complicated feelings about the engagement
jokes.explanation: Very quick, very good. Annie's 'No, I'm not!' is a perfect honest slip — she's happy for Lillian but her first instinct corrects the lie. Well-timed, character-specific, economical.

jokes.text: Annie's mom has painted a large portrait of Wynonna Judd: 'Wynonna Judd. / That's really good. / Painting those giant bangs was a royal pain in my can. / And those teeth! I should have painted her mouth shut.'
jokes.setup: We cut to Annie's parents' house; a large Wynonna Judd portrait is on the wall
jokes.punchline: 'I should have painted her mouth shut' — Annie's mom's critique of her own subject is a funny piece of casual cruelty toward a celebrity she apparently admires enough to paint
jokes.explanation: Annie's mom is immediately established as a wonderfully specific character. 'Royal pain in my can' is a great period-appropriate old-lady phrase, and 'I should have painted her mouth shut' about a portrait you painted yourself is a classic non-sequitur of unconscious cruelty.

jokes.text: Annie's mom forgot she signed up to speak at AA tonight: 'I keep telling you, you're not supposed to go to those things. / Only because I've never had a drink.'
jokes.setup: Annie's mom keeps attending AA meetings even though she's apparently never had a drink
jokes.punchline: 'Only because I've never had a drink' — the reason she's not an alcoholic is not that she has good values or strong willpower, but simply because she's never tried alcohol. Implies she would absolutely be one.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. 'Only because I've never had a drink' recontextualizes the entire AA subplot in one breath — this woman attends AA not because she recovered, but because she simply never started. The implication (that she WOULD be one) is funnier than any explicit statement. Perfect character economy and originality.

jokes.text: Annie's mom recounts an AA story: 'This gentleman who started blow-jobbing to get crack. His name is Marvin Johnson...' / 'Mom, anonymous. You keep... It's no names.'
jokes.setup: Annie's mom wants to share an inspiring AA story; the meeting is supposed to be anonymous
jokes.punchline: She starts with 'blow-jobbing to get crack' and immediately names the person — both violations (the content AND the anonymity) land simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Double violation joke — the story is shockingly explicit AND she names the person. Annie's weary 'anonymous, it's no names' is the perfect straight-man response. The mom's complete guilelessness makes it land.

jokes.text: 'Forget it. Marvin J. Whatever. / Too late.'
jokes.setup: Annie has corrected the mom about anonymity; mom tries to course-correct
jokes.punchline: 'Too late' — Annie's flat assessment that partial anonymization (Marvin J.) after full identification (Marvin Johnson) is useless
jokes.explanation: 'Too late' is a small but perfectly calibrated beat — the timing of Annie's delivery is everything here. The escalation (full name → Marvin J. → 'Too late') is well-structured.

jokes.text: Mom's conclusion: 'Well, he became a gay prostitute. And he realized that he had hit his bottom. And I have been thinking, honey, that maybe this is your bottom.'
jokes.setup: Mom is narrating the arc of Marvin J.'s story as an inspiration for Annie
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'gay prostitute crack addict' to 'this is your bottom, Annie' — delivered with complete maternal warmth — is both darkly funny and surprisingly cutting. 'Hit his bottom' also carries an unintentional double meaning in context.
jokes.explanation: The punchline — 'maybe this is your bottom' applied to Annie — is a great dark comedy beat. Mom genuinely means it as a compliment, which makes it land harder. 'Hitting bottom is a good thing' is hilariously delivered as sincere encouragement. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Mom complains about dad's new wife Barb: 'Thanks to that new whore, Barb. / They've been married 12 years. / Okay. But she's still a whore. / I'm sure she greets him in the evening, beaver first.'
jokes.setup: Mom mentions she goes everywhere alone since the divorce
jokes.punchline: 'I'm sure she greets him in the evening, beaver first' — the specificity of the image is both vulgar and completely in-character for this woman who has apparently spent 12 years stewing on this
jokes.explanation: Annie's mom is a great character and 'beaver first' is a genuinely surprising image. The comedic logic is sound: she's jealous, she's been stewing, and her brain goes immediately to the most vulgar possible explanation for her ex-husband's happiness. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'I bet she got that car by giving your dad something sexually. 'Cause there was one thing I would never do, and I'm sure Barb is a champion at it. / It's called a "chicken coop." Of course it is. / You start at the back and you peck your way to the front like you have a beak. And then you end up with two eggs in your mouth.'
jokes.setup: Mom has established Barb as a sexual schemer; now she's detailing Barb's supposed technique
jokes.punchline: The 'chicken coop' — an entirely invented sex act described in vivid farm animal metaphor — is an escalating absurdist masterpiece. 'Of course it is' from Annie is the perfect straight-man puncture.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in this reel by a significant margin. The 'chicken coop' is a perfect construction: entirely invented, described with specific physical detail ('you peck your way to the front like you have a beak'), escalating to the absurdist endpoint of 'two eggs in your mouth.' Annie's 'of course it is' is a masterclass in straight-man timing. The fact that the mom KNOWS about this act she claims she'd never do — and can describe it in farm-animal detail — is the dark, implicit subtext that makes it land even harder. 'He grew up on a farm' as the capper. Near-legendary joke, among the best in the film.

jokes.text: Annie arrives at the engagement party with what appears to be a very beat-up old car: 'Holy shit.' [pause] 'Ohh. Valet. Perfect.' [pause] 'Sorry. Needs a wash.' [pause] 'You have to punch it a few times.'
jokes.setup: Annie pulls up to what is clearly a very fancy country club or estate for Lillian's engagement party
jokes.punchline: The contrast between the upscale setting and Annie's apparently terrible, broken, dirty car — requiring her to apologize to the valet and explain how to operate it — is a sustained visual comedy bit
jokes.explanation: Classic fish-out-of-water visual comedy. The escalation — 'needs a wash' → 'you have to punch it a few times' — works well. Character-appropriate because we now understand Annie's financial state. The 'holy shit' reaction to the valet is a good beat.

jokes.text: Rita (Lillian's cousin with three boys) describes her sons: 'They are disgusting. They smell, they are sticky, they say things that are horrible, and there is semen all over everything, okay? I cracked a blanket in half. Do you get where I'm going with that? I cracked it in half.'
jokes.setup: Rita is introduced as a mother of three boys who are 'so cute'
jokes.punchline: 'I cracked a blanket in half' — the specific, horrifying detail about teenage sons and their blankets is an escalating escalation from 'sticky' and 'semen everywhere' to a singular concrete image
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the engagement party section. Rita's escalating description of teenage boy grossness climaxes with 'I cracked a blanket in half' — an image so specific and horrifying that it generates a big laugh from its pure commitment. 'Do you get where I'm going with that? I cracked it in half.' The repetition doubles down perfectly. High impact.

jokes.text: Becca and husband Kevin finish each other's sentences about their honeymoon at Disney World: 'We went on a sweetheart honeymoon.' / 'Disney World.' / 'Disney World.' / 'We finish each other's—' / 'Sentences. Sorry.' / 'Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Becca and Kevin are introduced as newlyweds who are sweet but perhaps cloying
jokes.punchline: The sentence-finishing itself becomes the joke — they finish each other's sentences about finishing each other's sentences, then both apologize simultaneously. Disney World as the honeymoon destination is also a minor laugh.
jokes.explanation: Competent character comedy. The self-referential sentence-finishing is a nice touch. Disney World as a honeymoon is a low-key joke about the couple's uncoolness. Works but isn't special.

jokes.text: Annie is introduced to Becca, then Becca gestures to a random man and asks if he's Annie's husband — Annie: 'No, no, no, no, no. I don't know him. I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Annie is single and arriving alone at a couples-heavy engagement party
jokes.punchline: Becca's inadvertent exposure of Annie's aloneness — assuming the nearest man is her partner — and Annie's emphatic 'I don't know him, I'm sorry' is a small cringe beat
jokes.explanation: Minor embarrassment beat. Works as texture for Annie's social situation at the party but isn't a strong joke on its own.

jokes.text: Annie explains to Becca she's here alone; Becca awkwardly tries to restart the introduction: 'Let's start it again. I'm Becca. Rewind.' — Kevin: 'You don't have a husband. / Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Becca has accidentally highlighted Annie's singleness; she tries to fix it
jokes.punchline: Kevin's flat correction 'You don't have a husband' — completing the restart but inserting the problem back in — is a great accidental doubling of the cringe
jokes.explanation: Kevin accidentally making it worse with 'you don't have a husband' during Becca's attempted reset is a good cringe escalation. His flat delivery makes it land.

jokes.text: Megan introduces herself to Annie while dealing with her grandmother's wine: 'Hey. Hey. It's going great. It's going great. I'm on the mend. I just got some pins in my legs. Believe it or not, pins in my legs, I can still do this. Right?'
jokes.setup: Megan is introduced at the engagement party; she intercepts her grandmother and starts talking to Annie
jokes.punchline: Megan's immediate disclosure of her post-surgery pins ('I can still do this' — presumably demonstrating a physical feat) is a baffling, confident, unsolicited overshare that establishes her character instantly
jokes.explanation: Megan McCarthy is a great character and her introduction — immediately discussing her pins and demonstrating physical capability — is a perfect character introduction beat. 'I can still do this. Right?' shows her need for validation from a stranger she just met.

jokes.text: Megan describes falling off a cruise ship: 'I fell off a cruise ship, but I'm back. / Took a hard, hard, violent fall. Kind of pinballed down. Hit a lot of railings, broke a lot of shit. / I'm not going to say I survived, I'm going to say I thrived.'
jokes.setup: Megan has established she has pins in her legs from an accident
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not going to say I survived, I'm going to say I thrived' — after describing a catastrophic 'pinball' fall off a cruise ship, Megan's motivational reframe is both absurd and very funny
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest character jokes in the reel. The escalating description of the fall ('pinballed down, hit a lot of railings, broke a lot of shit') builds beautifully to 'I'm not going to say I survived, I'm going to say I thrived' — a motivational-poster non sequitur delivered with Megan's characteristic confidence. The line is quotable and perfectly character-specific. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Megan describes her connection with a dolphin during the cruise ship fall: 'I met a dolphin down there. And I swear to God, that dolphin looked not at me, but into my soul... And he said, "I'm saving you, Megan." Not with his mouth, but he said it, I'm assuming, telepathically.'
jokes.setup: Megan has described surviving the fall; now she's detailing the spiritual aftermath
jokes.punchline: 'Not with his mouth, but he said it, I'm assuming, telepathically' — the qualifier is perfect. Megan is being careful to be accurate about the nature of the dolphin communication.
jokes.explanation: The dolphin sequence is exceptional. 'Not with his mouth, but he said it, I'm assuming, telepathically' is a brilliantly precise qualifier — Megan is being careful to be accurate, which makes the absurdism even more surreal. The 'I'm assuming' is the key word: she's not certain about the telepathy, just offering her best guess. This is Melissa McCarthy at her best — total commitment to deranged logic. Very high character integration, originality, and quotability.

jokes.text: Megan sees a man she doesn't know: 'I'm glad he's single, because I'm going to climb that like a tree.'
jokes.setup: Megan has assumed the nearby man is Annie's boyfriend; Annie corrects her ('He's not, I'm not, he's not')
jokes.punchline: 'I'm going to climb that like a tree' — Megan's immediate sexual interest in the stranger, expressed as a physical verb ('climb'), is a funny expression of her aggressive, unselfconscious personality
jokes.explanation: 'Climb that like a tree' is a very quotable line — it's specific, visual, and aggressive. Megan's confidence and physicality make it funnier than a standard 'he's hot' comment.

jokes.text: Introduction of Helen — Lillian calls her 'literally joined at the hip' with Dougie's boss, then Annie tries to claim the same closeness: 'Which is good, because so are we.'
jokes.setup: Lillian introduces Helen and notes how close she and Dougie's boss are.
jokes.punchline: Annie's immediate competitive bid for equal closeness with Lillian — 'which is good, because so are we' — is a jealousy flag delivered with performative casualness.
jokes.explanation: Annie's competitive response to Helen is both funny in the moment and significant for the film's larger arc. Gets a rewatch bonus because this is the first seed of the Helen-Annie rivalry. The delivery of 'so are we' as a cheerful assertion while clearly feeling threatened is good character work.

jokes.text: Lillian's dad: 'So much so that you two should get married right now and save me a shitload of money. Dad. Everybody always laughs at that, but I'm not joking. I'm not joking.'
jokes.setup: Lillian's dad is giving a toast about how much he loves Doug
jokes.punchline: The 'everybody always laughs at that, but I'm not joking' — the classic meta-joke of the person whose joke is mistaken for a joke — is funny because it's both a dad joke AND a sincere complaint about wedding costs
jokes.explanation: 'Everybody always laughs at that, but I'm not joking' is a satisfying meta beat. It's a recognizable type (the dad who makes the same joke at every event) but executed with enough specificity to work.

jokes.text: Helen's engagement party speech: recounting a trip to Miami with Lillian, 'I shared things with you that I've never shared with anyone. And you made me realize how I can trust people again.' — delivered with intense intimacy to the entire room, then: 'Lillian, you are my best friend.'
jokes.setup: Annie has given a brief, warm but simple toast; Helen takes the floor and delivers an escalating emotional monologue
jokes.punchline: Helen's speech is designed to unseat Annie as Lillian's best friend — 'Lillian, you are my best friend' — delivered with perfect performance-level sincerity after Annie's toast. The cringe comes from watching Annie realize what's happening.
jokes.explanation: This is the reel's most significant structural comedy moment — the implicit rivalry between Annie and Helen is established through Helen's speech, which both outclasses Annie's and directly claims Annie's role. The comedy is in the cruelty of the implicit competition and Annie's silent realization. High character integration for both characters. Strong rewatch value as the film's main comic conflict begins here.

jokes.text: Helen's speech: 'And, Dougly... I'm sorry, inside joke.'
jokes.setup: Helen is wrapping up her toast and addresses the groom
jokes.punchline: 'Dougly' — an intimate nickname for Dougie — with the added twist of 'I'm sorry, inside joke' — signals to the room (and to Annie) that Helen has a private intimacy with this couple that Annie, the childhood best friend, doesn't have
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedy-through-subtext moments in the reel. 'Dougly... I'm sorry, inside joke' is devastating — it's a flex disguised as an apology. Helen deploys the inside joke knowing full well what it communicates: I am closer to this couple than you are. The economy is extraordinary — two words and an apology do the work of an entire scene. The cringe lands fully on Annie (and the audience) because we understand exactly what's happening. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Annie's heartfelt MOH speech is immediately one-upped by Helen launching into an eloquent, polished counter-speech the moment Annie tries to wrap up
jokes.setup: Annie delivers a sincere, slightly clunky maid-of-honor speech and says 'Well, that concludes the speeches for the night'
jokes.punchline: Helen immediately stands and says 'One last thing' — launching a superior, more polished speech that completely overshadows Annie's
jokes.explanation: The setup is perfectly structured: Annie's speech is earnest but generic, her 'that concludes' wrap signals relief — and then Helen immediately seizes the floor with something better. The joke is rooted in pure character rivalry: Helen doesn't need to be malicious, she just IS more polished, which is worse. Strong character integration because this dynamic is the film's spine.

jokes.text: Helen name-drops a recent trip to Thailand with her husband Perry to deliver a Lillian-themed inspirational quote in the middle of an engagement party speech
jokes.setup: Helen is ostensibly giving a warm speech about friendship with Lillian
jokes.punchline: She casually drops a Thailand trip and attributes a poetic quote to Thai culture — the wealth and effortless sophistication are played completely straight, making them funnier
jokes.explanation: The casual wealth flex — Thailand, husband Perry, exotic wisdom — is a sharp character note. Helen isn't trying to be showy; she just IS showy, which is funnier. Moderate craft because the joke is in the subtext rather than any sharp construction.

jokes.text: Annie, trying to regain the floor from Helen, announces she'll say something in Spanish — then delivers an extended, stumbling attempt at a Spanish speech that goes on for over 20 seconds
jokes.setup: Annie mentions she and Lillian took Spanish together in school, implying she'll say something charming and bilingual
jokes.punchline: She then fumbles through broken, barely-coherent Spanish for an agonizingly long time while the room watches in silence — the transcript gap [25:13] to [25:39] is the joke itself
jokes.explanation: The 26-second gap in dialogue IS the joke — Annie is visibly floundering in Spanish at a formal party, and the audience's discomfort accumulates with every second of silence. The setup (she mentioned Spanish class) makes the failure feel earned rather than random. High character integration: Annie's desire to compete with Helen while being completely outgunned is her core arc. One of the reel's best sustained cringe beats.

jokes.text: Annie's Spanish speech payoff: 'I feel so close to you and can trust you. You are my angel and soul mate. And I feel I can communicate with you with simply a look.'
jokes.setup: After 26 seconds of fumbling Spanish, the room anticipates something either impressive or disastrously wrong
jokes.punchline: What comes out is a perfectly translated but utterly generic, over-the-top romantic sentiment — the content is hilariously banal given the buildup
jokes.explanation: Works as a payoff to joke #3 — after all that struggle, the content is just cheesy platitudes. The comedy is in the gap between effort and result. Slightly less sharp than the buildup itself.

jokes.text: Annie and Helen simultaneously try to take Lillian's glass after the speeches, both grabbing for it — a small physical moment of competing for Lillian's attention
jokes.setup: Both Annie and Helen are vying for Lillian's approval throughout the party
jokes.punchline: They collide over something as trivial as taking her glass, reducing their rivalry to a petty physical squabble — 'Here, I'll take that. I'll take that. Yep, I got it.'
jokes.explanation: A compact visual/physical gag that efficiently summarizes the Annie-Helen dynamic in a single moment. Not a big laugh but a smart piece of character comedy. The dialogue 'I got it' is the perfect petty capstone.

jokes.text: Annie sings 'That's What Friends Are For' to Lillian at the party — the camera reaction and the fact that she is performing this earnestly while clearly losing the social battle makes it devastating
jokes.setup: Annie has just been thoroughly outclassed by Helen's speech and the glass-grab; she is trying to salvage her standing with Lillian
jokes.punchline: She launches into a full Dionne Warwick song performance — sincere but socially catastrophic
jokes.explanation: The song choice is perfect — it's the most earnest, sincere possible response to losing a social fight, which makes it both painful and funny. Annie singing this FULLY, with feeling, while the party presumably watches awkwardly, is a great cringe set piece. Strong character integration: this IS Annie — she doubles down on sincerity when she's losing.

jokes.text: 'Man, engagement parties rule. It made me feel awesome, like I can go out and catch another dude to marry.'
jokes.setup: Post-party debrief; characters are reflecting on the evening
jokes.punchline: Megan's takeaway from an engagement party is entirely self-centered and weirdly predatory — 'catch another dude to marry' — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Megan's character voice is perfectly deployed here — she hears 'engagement party' and processes it entirely through her own romantic ambitions. 'Catch another dude' is a great verb choice; it makes marriage sound like pest control. Efficient and character-specific.

jokes.text: Annie trying to diplomatically express her jealousy of Helen to Lillian, completely failing to articulate it: 'What? I'm just like... I don't know. She's in your wedding and you've only known her eight months, though, right? Come on. Get it out, get it all out.'
jokes.setup: Lillian asks what Annie thinks of Helen; Annie wants to voice her jealousy but knows she shouldn't
jokes.punchline: Annie's answer is a stream of half-starts, stutters, and deflections — she can't even complete a jealous sentence, while Lillian cheers her on sarcastically
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe beat. Annie's inability to say what she means is a good character note, and Lillian's 'Get it out, get it all out' is a nice sisterly tease. Slightly bloated — the joke runs a bit long for what it delivers.

jokes.text: Oh. Hi, I'm Helen. You live in Milwaukee? I'm sorry.
jokes.setup: Annie has just agreed to get to know Helen as a favor to Lillian; Helen immediately appears
jokes.punchline: Helen's very first words to Annie are an accidental insult — 'You live in Milwaukee? I'm sorry' — delivered with genuine, oblivious sympathy
jokes.explanation: Four words — 'You live in Milwaukee? I'm sorry' — perfectly encapsulate Helen's character: she's not being deliberately cruel, she genuinely pities people below her social station, which is funnier. The timing is impeccable (Helen materializes the moment they agreed to be friends). Excellent economy — this is a lot of character work in very few words. High quotability.

jokes.text: Annie falling / stumbling off the curb in front of the cop — described by his line 'I'm not drunk. I told you.' and her response 'So, you are just a terrible sober driver?'
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to prove to Officer Rhodes that she isn't drunk
jokes.punchline: His comeback: 'So you are just a terrible sober driver?' — the inversion that being sober makes her driving MORE embarrassing
jokes.explanation: The punchline is sharp and efficient — 'just a terrible sober driver' reframes her defense as a worse admission. Good economy, good structure. The cop's dry wit is immediately charming and sets up the romance well.

jokes.text: Annie attempting a sobriety field test — the transcript gap [28:15] to [28:43] where she is apparently doing something physical (likely a sobriety walk or one-leg stand) while the cop watches
jokes.setup: Annie says 'Hey, look. If I was drunk, would I be able to do this?' and proceeds to demonstrate sobriety
jokes.punchline: The 28-second gap suggests an extended, likely embarrassing physical demonstration; his response 'Stop it. Stop it. Please, stop. I believe you. You are not drunk.' suggests it was absurd enough to be convincing purely out of pity
jokes.explanation: The gap is the joke — whatever Annie does is visually funny enough to make a cop say 'stop it, please stop' before conceding. The payoff line 'I believe you, you are not drunk' has a lovely double meaning: I believe you AND I'm frightened of what you're doing. Visual comedy inferred from context.

jokes.text: 'Oh. Cake Baby.' — Officer Rhodes recognizes Annie's former bakery
jokes.setup: Annie mentions she used to have a bakery on Ashley Street
jokes.punchline: The name 'Cake Baby' — which is revealed to have had a sign with Annie's face on it — is inherently, absurdly funny as a business name
jokes.explanation: The name 'Cake Baby' is doing a lot of work — it's sweet, slightly absurd, and paired with a sign that features Annie's face, it paints a vivid picture of well-intentioned earnestness. The cop's flat delivery 'Oh. Cake Baby.' is perfect deadpan. Good economy — the whole failed bakery backstory is compressed into two words.

jokes.text: 'I used to get served by this tall, broad guy, with, like, a wormy face.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes is reminiscing fondly about Cake Baby, describing the person who served him
jokes.punchline: 'Wormy face' — an unexpected, oddly specific and vivid insult delivered completely casually, as if it's a neutral descriptor
jokes.explanation: 'Wormy face' is a brilliantly specific phrase — not 'ugly' or 'weird-looking' but *wormy*, which conjures a very particular image. The fact that it's delivered as a neutral physical description, not an insult, makes it funnier. Good economy and originality in word choice.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, that was my boyfriend.' — Annie reveals the wormy-faced guy was her ex
jokes.setup: Rhodes describes the 'tall, broad guy with the wormy face' who served him
jokes.punchline: Annie flatly confirms it was her boyfriend — the reveal recontextualizes 'wormy face' as now being about her romantic life
jokes.explanation: The one-beat pause implied before 'Yeah, that was my boyfriend' is perfect. Annie's flat delivery absorbs the insult without commentary, which is funnier than if she'd reacted. The reveal lands because we weren't expecting Rhodes's casual description to have personal stakes for Annie.

jokes.text: 'What a dick. I'm glad I never tipped him.'
jokes.setup: Annie reveals her boyfriend abandoned her when her business failed
jokes.punchline: Rhodes's response escalates from sympathy to retroactive petty revenge — 'I'm glad I never tipped him' — as if withholding a tip years ago was a moral act
jokes.explanation: This is one of the reel's best lines. 'What a dick' is good — 'I'm glad I never tipped him' is great. The escalation from moral judgment to petty financial vindication, delivered as a complete non sequitur, is perfectly constructed. It also characterizes Rhodes as funny and endearing in one line. Excellent economy, strong structure, highly quotable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor — not quite legendary but genuinely excellent.

jokes.text: Bill Cozbi — 'with a Z' — 'Different guy. Yeah.' exchange
jokes.setup: Rhodes gives Annie the name of a body shop contact — Bill Cozbi
jokes.punchline: The name sounds like Bill Cosby; both characters immediately acknowledge it and have to clarify it's spelled with a Z; Rhodes adds 'don't mention the whole Bill Cosby thing to him, it drives him nuts'
jokes.explanation: A functional name-pun joke. The 'drives him nuts' extension is a good beat. Post-2014 Cosby revelations have dated this significantly, which affects the earned_vs_cheap score. At time of release this was a clean, light wordplay joke that worked as a palette cleanser in the scene.

jokes.text: 'We are not all bad. / What? / I was just saying, we are not all bad! / Actually, the rest of them are, but not me. I'm the best of them.'
jokes.setup: Annie is walking away; Rhodes calls out a parting remark
jokes.punchline: He shouts it twice across the distance, then escalates it to 'the rest of them are [bad], but not me. I'm the best of them.' — a quietly grandiose self-assessment
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'we're not all bad' to 'I'm the best of them' is a lovely character moment — Rhodes is funny, modest, and weirdly confident all at once. The shouting-across-distance setup adds a physical comedy layer. This is excellent romantic-comedy character writing: he's charming without being slick.

jokes.text: Annie and Helen's tennis 'get to know each other' session devolving into a passive-aggressive debate about whether people change, while ostensibly playing tennis
jokes.setup: Lillian has asked Annie and Helen to hang out and bond; they're playing tennis
jokes.punchline: Their conversation quickly becomes a philosophical argument ('I think we change all the time / I think we stay the same') that is clearly a proxy war about Lillian's friendship — neither will give an inch
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between what they're saying (philosophy of change) and what they mean (you're new, I was here first). It's a bit drawn out and the actual lines aren't particularly sharp, but it sets up the stepkid interruption well and characterizes both women efficiently.

jokes.text: Helen's stepchildren interrupting with 'Fuck off, Helen.'
jokes.setup: Helen cheerfully calls out to her approaching stepchildren during the tennis scene
jokes.punchline: One of them responds with a flat, completely unapologetic 'Fuck off, Helen' — delivered as casually as a greeting
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words do enormous work. Helen's slightly forced warmth toward her husband's children has been subtly established, and the child's blistering dismissal punctures it completely. The 'Okay. Put a quarter in the swear-jar.' response is the perfect Helen beat: she absorbs it with grace and control. Highly quotable, huge laugh moment. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its precision and shock.

jokes.text: Helen's clarifications: 'Step-kids. Step.' and 'Excuse me, my husband's kids.'
jokes.setup: Helen introduces her children during the tennis scene
jokes.punchline: She immediately corrects herself twice — 'Step-kids. Step.' — distancing herself from them even as she tries to seem warm; a tiny involuntary reveal of her real feelings
jokes.explanation: The double correction — 'Step-kids. Step.' (then later 'my husband's kids') — is a great character note. She needs you to know these are not her children. The more she says it, the more it reveals. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: "Okay. Put a quarter in the swear-jar." — Helen's response to being told to fuck off by her stepkid
jokes.setup: Stepkid just told Helen to fuck off in front of Annie
jokes.punchline: Helen responds with the most mild, procedural parenting correction possible — as though it's a routine occurrence
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic control. Helen neither escalates nor breaks down — she applies the mildest possible sanction, suggesting this is simply a routine part of her life. The juxtaposition of the vulgarity and the response is excellent. Rewatch value because it cracks open Helen's domestic reality.

jokes.text: 'Carol! Get your shit together, Carol!'
jokes.setup: Annie is playing tennis, apparently against an unseen opponent named Carol
jokes.punchline: Annie erupts at Carol with disproportionate competitive aggression, completely out of nowhere — a sudden tonal shift from the polite Helen conversation
jokes.explanation: The explosive non sequitur of 'Get your shit together, Carol!' is funny partly because of its specificity (why Carol? who is Carol?) and partly because of the intensity — Annie apparently takes this recreational tennis very seriously. Good quotability and economy.

jokes.text: 'I've seen better tennis playing in a tampon commercial.'
jokes.setup: Annie is watching/competing in tennis; she delivers a trash-talk line
jokes.punchline: The 'tampon commercial' simile — an oddly specific and vivid insult that equates bad tennis with the performatively athletic women in feminine hygiene ads
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The 'tampon commercial' reference is startlingly specific and vivid — everyone immediately pictures those slow-motion women in white doing yoga, and the insult lands because it's accurate AND unexpected. The craft is in the precision of the image. High originality, excellent economy, very quotable. Earns its 8+ score.

jokes.text: Annie's reaction beat immediately after delivering 'tampon commercial' trash talk
jokes.setup: Annie delivers an aggressive trash-talk line ('I've seen better tennis playing in a tampon commercial')
jokes.punchline: 'Umm...' — the transcript shows only 'Umm...' after the line, implying Annie immediately second-guesses herself or the line lands to dead silence
jokes.explanation: The 'Umm...' that follows the trash talk is a small but effective beat — it suggests Annie surprised even herself. Works as a tag to joke #23 rather than a standalone.

jokes.text: Annie confronting her roommates: 'I've been thinking, and... Brynn needs to start paying rent. That's it. She's been here long enough.'
jokes.setup: Scene shifts to Annie's apartment; she delivers an ultimatum about rent
jokes.punchline: Brynn immediately explains she's on a tourist visa and 'technically, I'm only allowed to tour' — a brilliantly literal interpretation of visa status
jokes.explanation: Brynn's 'technically, I'm only allowed to tour' is a great absurdist reading of legal language. The literal interpretation of 'tourist' is both logically consistent and completely unhelpful, which is the ideal comedic response to Annie's frustration.

jokes.text: 'I have no way of earning money, unless I just go and prostitute down on the street. / I don't want you to do that, no. / Hello, fellas. Here I am.' (Brynn's prostitution roleplay)
jokes.setup: Brynn claims she has no way to earn money on a tourist visa
jokes.punchline: She immediately volunteers streetwalking as the alternative and then acts it out with 'Hello, fellas. Here I am.' — played with utter cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: Brynn's cheerful willingness to perform prostitution roleplay mid-argument — with zero self-awareness — is perfectly in character. 'Hello, fellas. Here I am.' is quotable and delivered with wonderful obliviousness. The roommates' absurdist dynamic is established quickly and effectively.

jokes.text: 'Put your American sausage in my English McMuffin.'
jokes.setup: Brynn is playfully roleplaying as a streetwalker; Gil apparently extends the bit
jokes.punchline: Brynn's British-accented sexual solicitation line, framed as a fast-food metaphor — 'American sausage / English McMuffin' — is both a pun and a character-specific absurdist riff
jokes.explanation: The nationality-based food metaphor is clever — 'American sausage / English McMuffin' is a culturally specific, clean, funny double entendre. The fact that Brynn is British makes the character integration strong. It's the kind of line that gets quoted. Earns high quotability.

jokes.text: Gil reading Annie's diary — 'At first, I did not know that it was your diary. I thought it was a very sad, hand-written book.'
jokes.setup: Annie confronts Gil about reading her diary/journal
jokes.punchline: Gil's defense: he thought it was 'a very sad, hand-written book' — the description is both an accidental insult (it's so sad it reads like fiction) and a perfect absurdist explanation
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. 'I thought it was a very sad, hand-written book' is exceptional on multiple levels: (1) it's a devastating accidental burn on Annie's life, (2) Gil's logic is internally consistent — why would someone write that, it must be fiction — (3) the specificity of 'hand-written' as a subcategory of book is absurdly pedantic. The line does enormous character and comedic work simultaneously. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and arguably surpasses it in originality.

jokes.text: Gil's defense: 'I think, before you make those sort of demands, you need to, maybe, think about putting a note on your door saying, Do not come into my room, read my diary and wear my clothes.'
jokes.setup: Annie tells Gil not to go in her room and read her diary
jokes.punchline: Gil escalates the list of violations — 'read my diary AND wear my clothes' — casually revealing he has also been wearing her clothes, as if that's a normal addendum
jokes.explanation: The escalation from diary to clothes is perfectly constructed — 'and wear my clothes' is delivered as an afterthought, as if clothing-theft is the lesser violation. The implication that this requires a *specific written note* is also funny. Excellent structure and character integration: Gil's oblivious entitlement is a great comedic persona.

jokes.text: Annie, Helen, and the bridesmaids at the Brazilian restaurant — 'I got to say, Annie's really good at this. She always drags me to the weirdest places and the food is always incredible.'
jokes.setup: The group is hesitant about the unfamiliar neighborhood restaurant
jokes.punchline: Becca's warm, genuine endorsement of Annie's weird food choices is a small character moment that also sets up the bridesmaids dinner comedically
jokes.explanation: More of a character beat than a joke — it's warm and functional, establishing Annie as the group's quirky food expert. Not particularly funny on its own but sets up the group dynamic well.

jokes.text: Annie's reaction shot/pause after the roommate explains she needs a note specifying "do not wear my clothes"
jokes.setup: The roommate lists the three things Annie needs to put on a sign to protect herself
jokes.punchline: Annie's implied expression of resigned defeat — realizing her home life is simply this
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat building Annie's pathetic home life. Not a joke on its own but part of the comedic rhythm.

jokes.text: 'Whoa! Somebody likes Brazilian food.' — reaction to one of the bridesmaids immediately and enthusiastically diving in
jokes.setup: The group sits down at the Brazilian restaurant and food arrives
jokes.punchline: Someone dives into the food so eagerly that it merits a 'Whoa!' from Annie — the implied visual of this person's enthusiasm is funnier than any line
jokes.explanation: A light, functional reaction beat. Without seeing the visual, the comedic weight is limited on transcript alone, but it signals a funny physical moment.

jokes.text: 'This is such a stone-cold pack of weirdos, and I'm so proud.'
jokes.setup: Lillian toasts her bridesmaids at the Brazilian restaurant
jokes.punchline: 'Stone-cold pack of weirdos' — she toasts them with an insult-compliment that's both affectionate and genuinely accurate
jokes.explanation: A quotable character line. 'Stone-cold pack of weirdos' is a great phrase — the 'stone-cold' intensifier makes it funnier. Works as both a laugh and an affectionate character moment.

jokes.text: 'If you go alone, people might think you're a prostitute. / Maybe.'
jokes.setup: Rita is trying to convince Annie to let her set her up with a date for the wedding
jokes.punchline: Rita warns that going alone means people will think Annie is a prostitute; Annie responds with 'Maybe.' — not denying it
jokes.explanation: Annie's 'Maybe.' is a one-word punchline that earns a big laugh through self-deprecation and subverted expectation — we expect her to deny it. The resigned acceptance makes it funnier than any comeback would. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: Helen proudly not eating meat at the churrasco: 'It's not good to eat a big meal before a fitting. I feel a bit bloated, so...' / 'Not me.' / 'No? No. Physically, I don't bloat.' / 'Lucky. That is lucky.' / 'It's a gift.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is enthusiastically eating at the Brazilian churrasco; Helen abstains
jokes.punchline: Helen reveals she 'physically doesn't bloat' — delivered as a sincere statement — and calls it 'a gift,' completing the portrait of her effortless, infuriating superiority
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I don't bloat' to 'it's a gift' is perfectly calibrated Helen. She's not bragging — she's just stating a fact about her superior physiology, which is funnier than bragging would be. Extremely high character integration: this is the definitive Helen character note. The Annie 'Lucky. That is lucky.' underplay is also well-executed.

jokes.text: Rita's story: 'The other night, I'm slaving away, making a beautiful dinner for my family. My youngest boy comes in and says he wants to order a pizza. I said, No, we're not ordering pizza tonight. He goes, Mom, why don't you go and fuck yourself? He's nine.'
jokes.setup: Rita is talking about wanting to get married and have kids in a wistful, idealized way
jokes.punchline: 'He goes, Mom, why don't you go and fuck yourself? He's nine.' — delivered flatly, as a matter of fact, to contrast with Becca's romantic idealization of motherhood
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the reel. The structure is immaculate: Becca's earnest wish for children and motherhood is immediately demolished by Rita's flat anecdote, capped with the killer 'He's nine.' The two-word kicker is the best use of economy in the transcript. It works as a subversive response to romantic idealization, it's perfectly Rita (exhausted, unsentimental mom), and 'He's nine' has become a quotable touchstone. This competes with the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Annie proposing a Paris-themed bridal shower: champagne, little cookies that say 'Lillian and Dougie,' chocolate fondue, 'cheese from the nice part of the store'
jokes.setup: Annie pitches a romantic, budget-conscious Paris-themed shower
jokes.punchline: 'Cheese from the nice part of the store' — the qualifier reveals Annie's financial reality while trying to sound aspirational
jokes.explanation: 'The nice part of the store' is a quietly brilliant class marker — it shows Annie's aspirations and limitations simultaneously. It's the detail that makes the whole Paris plan sweet and slightly sad. Good character integration.

jokes.text: "What about a Pixar-themed shower? And we all come dressed as our favorite Pixar character."
jokes.setup: Helen dismisses Annie's Paris theme as "been there, done that"; asks for other ideas
jokes.punchline: Becca contributes... a Pixar-themed bridal shower with costumes
jokes.explanation: Becca's Pixar idea is funny because it's said with total sincerity — she clearly thought this was a great idea going in. The gap between the earnestness and the appropriateness is the joke.

jokes.text: Megan proposing a Pixar-themed shower followed by a female fight club: 'We grease up, we pull in. Lillian doesn't know, so it's, Surprise! We're going to fight! We beat the shit out of her.'
jokes.setup: The bridesmaids are brainstorming shower themes; Megan throws out 'Pixar-themed' and then immediately escalates to 'Fight Club'
jokes.punchline: 'Lillian doesn't know, so it's, Surprise! We're going to fight! We just fucking attack.' — delivered with complete earnestness, as if this is a loving, festive option
jokes.explanation: Megan is the film's funniest character and this is a showcase moment. The escalation from Pixar to Fight Club, and the specificity of 'we grease up, we pull in' as shower planning is brilliantly absurd. 'Surprise! We're going to fight!' is a great line because Megan presents it as a *gift* to Lillian. The 'we just fucking attack' kicker is perfect. High originality, strong character integration. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: "And I'll just snowball on top of that, also Fight Club. Female fight club. We grease up, we pull in. Lillian doesn't know, so it's, 'Surprise! We're going to fight!'"
jokes.setup: Becca has proposed a Pixar-themed bridal shower; Megan decides to build on this
jokes.punchline: Megan pivots immediately to a female fight club where the guest of honor is ambushed with violence as a surprise party
jokes.explanation: "Surprise! We're going to fight!" and "We just fucking attack" are exceptional. The joke is in the total logic of Megan's worldview: this is a fun surprise to her. McCarthy's escalation — 'snowball on top of that,' the greasing up, the specificity of the attack — is brilliantly unhinged. High character integration: this is 100% Megan and nobody else. One of the best jokes in the reel. Earns its 8+ score decisively.

jokes.text: Rita's bachelorette speech: 'I'm at home with three boys all day, every day. What about the bachelorette party? I've got a new tube top, I want to cut the tags off. I'd like to take advantage of this opportunity.'
jokes.setup: The group is debating shower themes; Rita cuts in
jokes.punchline: 'I've got a new tube top, I want to cut the tags off' — the specificity of a saved tube top as a signal of pent-up maternal imprisonment is both funny and touching
jokes.explanation: The tube top detail is a perfect character note for Rita. The tags are still on — she's been waiting for a reason to wear it, and a bachelorette party is finally that reason. It's specific, economical, and completely true to her character as a mom desperate for a night out.

jokes.text: "That poor girl, Lillian, who we're all here for, is in the bathroom probably bawling her fucking eyes out. Because she's realizing, 'Holy shit! I've got to spend the rest of my life with Doug.' He's my brother. I love him. But he is a fucking asshole."
jokes.setup: The bridesmaids are debating shower themes while Lillian is in the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Megan delivers a stunning monologue theorizing Lillian is in the bathroom having a breakdown about marrying Doug, then confirms: he's her brother and an asshole
jokes.explanation: "He is a fucking asshole. I think we can all agree on that, right?" is a brilliant pivot — Megan defends Lillian's hypothetical grief, roasts her own brother, and then looks for consensus as though it's obvious. The reveal that she's the groom's sister reframes everything. The structure (concern → roast → familial clarification → 'we can all agree') is tight. Genuinely memorable.

jokes.text: Megan's speech about Lillian possibly crying in the bathroom because she's realized she has to spend her life with Doug, capped with 'He's my brother. I love him. But he is a fucking asshole. I think we can all agree on that, right?'
jokes.setup: Megan is making a point about why the bachelorette party matters
jokes.punchline: 'He's my brother. I love him. But he is a fucking asshole. I think we can all agree on that, right?' — casually throwing her own brother under the bus mid-party planning
jokes.explanation: The comma structure — 'I love him. But he is a fucking asshole.' — is classic deadpan and the 'I think we can all agree on that, right?' is a great closer. Megan characterizing her own brother this way at his fiancée's shower planning dinner is a great dark beat. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Annie attempting walk-in bridesmaids dress shopping — no appointment, no problem
jokes.setup: Annie leads the bridesmaids to the dress shop Belle en Blanc and proudly announces they're there to shop
jokes.punchline: The sales associate coldly informs her there are no walk-ins and the next appointment is seven weeks away — Annie's confidence immediately deflated
jokes.explanation: A functional setup for the Helen phone-call payoff. Annie's confidence is punctured quickly, which is good economical storytelling. The joke is mild on its own but necessary for what follows.

jokes.text: Helen makes one phone call and they're immediately buzzed in: 'Whitney? It's Helen. Helen Harris? Yeah! Hi! Hi. Oh, my God. Hi. Listen, I'll buzz you right in.'
jokes.setup: Annie has just been told there's a seven-week wait for walk-ins
jokes.punchline: Helen says one name on the phone and they are immediately admitted — the contrast with Annie's complete failure makes the class/social-capital gap land as the punchline
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition is sharp and efficiently executed. Annie's public humiliation followed by Helen's instant access via a single phone call — 'Whitney? It's Helen.' — is a perfect summation of their dynamic. High character integration. The 'Oh, my God. Hi!' from Whitney suggests Helen's social power is extraordinary.

jokes.text: Megan's fart/bodily eruption at the entrance to the elegant bridal boutique: 'I'm sorry, I want to apologize. I'm not even confident on which end that came out of.'
jokes.setup: The bridesmaids enter the ultra-refined Belle en Blanc bridal boutique
jokes.punchline: Megan immediately makes a grotesque noise/smell; she apologizes with 'I'm not even confident on which end that came out of' — adding ambiguity to the violation
jokes.explanation: The venue contrast (exquisite bridal boutique / Megan's body) is the setup; the punchline 'I'm not even confident on which end that came out of' is a great escalation because it makes the violation worse. Megan's matter-of-fact tone and the implicit visual are both strong. Highly quotable and a great Megan character moment.

jokes.text: Annie being dazzled by a Fritz Bernaise gown and Helen casually revealing the $800 dress is on sale
jokes.setup: The bridesmaids discover an expensive designer gown; Annie notes it's $800
jokes.punchline: Helen: 'Are you kidding? It's on sale.' — delivered with genuine surprise that Annie would even mention the price
jokes.explanation: A clean class-gap joke. Helen's 'Are you kidding? It's on sale' frames the $800 price tag as practically a bargain — the gap between her reality and Annie's is the joke. Functional, well-executed, not exceptional.

jokes.text: "Helen, this is $800." "Are you kidding? It's on sale."
jokes.setup: Helen is pushing the most expensive dress in the store; Annie objects to the price
jokes.punchline: Helen's "It's on sale" — delivered as though this resolves Annie's concern, while $800 on sale implies the original price was absurd
jokes.explanation: Classic class-gap comedy. Helen genuinely thinks "on sale" ends the debate. Good but familiar territory.

jokes.text: Lillian reveals Helen's friend is designing her wedding dress: 'Because guess who Helen is friends with and who's designing my wedding dress. Lady St. Petsois JuJu.'
jokes.setup: Annie suggests not upstaging Lillian with a fancy bridesmaid dress
jokes.punchline: Lillian reveals her own wedding dress is by 'Lady St. Petsois JuJu' — a designer name that is itself absurd-sounding enough to be funny
jokes.explanation: The designer name 'Lady St. Petsois JuJu' is deliberately absurd — it sounds like a parody of a French fashion house, which may be the point. Lillian's pride in it is part of the joke. Works well as a character beat showing how Helen's influence has permeated Lillian's wedding.

jokes.text: 'I just sent my measurements to France, y'all. / No, you didn't.'
jokes.setup: Lillian reveals she has a couture wedding dress designed in France
jokes.punchline: Rita's flat, disbelieving 'No, you didn't.' — a perfect friend response that's both funny and grounding
jokes.explanation: 'No, you didn't.' is three words doing big comedic work — it's the ideal 'down-to-earth friend' response to someone who has gone too fancy. The economy is excellent. It's relatable and precisely deployed.

jokes.text: 'Where were you when I was getting married?'
jokes.setup: Rita has just been told about the couture French wedding dress designer
jokes.punchline: Rita's question implies her own wedding was considerably less glamorous — delivered with genuine, slightly mournful envy
jokes.explanation: A compact character line that tells us everything about Rita's marriage and life in five words. The gentle pathos underneath it makes it funnier than a pure joke would be. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'Ladies, let's not decide on this bridesmaids' dress straight away. Let's let our bodies decide.' / 'Ladies, start your engines.'
jokes.setup: The shop manager tries to manage the excited, slightly chaotic bridesmaids
jokes.punchline: 'Let's let our bodies decide' and 'Ladies, start your engines' are both subtly patronizing phrases delivered with high-end retail cheerfulness — the contrast between the refined setting and the group's energy is the joke
jokes.explanation: The boutique manager's canned enthusiasm is a mild joke — 'let our bodies decide' and 'start your engines' are amusingly corporate wellness-speak applied to dress shopping. Functional but not a standout.

jokes.text: The bridal consultant builds up the Fritz Bernaise as one-of-a-kind with no question — and Annie immediately says 'There might be a question. I might... I might have a question.'
jokes.setup: The imperious consultant declares the Fritz Bernaise is THE dress with 'no question' — clearly expecting deference from the bridesmaids.
jokes.punchline: Annie timidly but persistently contradicts her, undercutting the consultant's authority with a meek but firm dissent.
