jokes.explanation: Classic Annie move — she can't quite capitulate to social pressure but can't fully assert herself either. The doubling of 'I might... I might have a question' captures her anxious hedging perfectly. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Annie's pitch for the alternative dress includes 'You can spread your legs apart' as a selling point.
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to make a practical, enthusiastic case for the cheaper dress, listing normal benefits like color, length, and movement.
jokes.punchline: 'You can spread your legs apart' — delivered as a completely sincere benefit, with no self-awareness of how it sounds.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Annie is completely earnest — she means 'freedom of movement' — and the phrase lands as an inadvertent double entendre. The deadpan delivery in a bridal boutique setting is perfect. Solid comedy economy.

jokes.text: The consultant has been building toward the Lady JuJu reveal — and when Lillian steps out in the two-year-old wedding dress, the entire bridal party's reaction is audible shock and reverence.
jokes.setup: The consultant has been pushing the Fritz Bernaise; now she produces a secret weapon — a vintage wedding dress — presumably to show how inferior the bridesmaids' dresses will look by comparison.
jokes.punchline: Everyone's genuine, overwhelmed reaction ('My God,' 'Holy shit! You look amazing') subverts the satirical frame — the dress actually IS stunning, derailing the scene's tension.
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the genuine emotional hijacking — a moment designed to be manipulative by the consultant accidentally produces real awe. It's a beat that sets up the food poisoning chaos to follow and gains meaning in retrospect.

jokes.text: 'That dress is so pretty it makes my stomach hurt.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is gushing about how beautiful Lillian looks in the wedding dress. 'It makes my stomach hurt' sounds like a hyperbolic compliment.
jokes.punchline: Given what's about to happen (mass food poisoning), this is a brilliant piece of dramatic irony — Annie's stomach literally IS about to hurt.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. It functions simultaneously as a sincere gush AND a perfect piece of dramatic irony — on first watch it's a funny throwaway, on rewatch it's a masterclass in foreshadowing-as-comedy. The economy is extraordinary: six words do double duty. The fact that it's delivered in Annie's earnest voice makes it land even harder.

jokes.text: 'Megan, are you okay?' — followed by a pause before Megan says 'I think... My dress was probably just tight.'
jokes.setup: Megan is visibly suffering from food poisoning in a pristine bridal boutique. The question 'are you okay?' is asked with obvious concern.
jokes.punchline: Megan's denial — 'My dress was probably just tight' — is a heroic piece of understatement. We can clearly see/infer she is NOT okay.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy for Megan — she is constitutionally incapable of admitting weakness. 'My dress was probably just tight' is both deeply in character and an excellent piece of denial comedy. The specificity of blaming the dress (rather than saying 'I'm fine') is what elevates it.

jokes.text: Helen says she had 'the same thing' as Megan and feels fine, implying Annie is to blame for the restaurant choice.
jokes.setup: Everyone is visibly getting sick. Helen's comment is ostensibly about the food poisoning.
jokes.punchline: The subtext is a dig at Annie — 'I feel fine' implies the sick people are weak, and positions Helen as smugly superior even during a mass illness event.
jokes.explanation: Competent character work — Helen's smugness is well-established, and her immunity to the poisoning (or claim thereof) fits perfectly. Not exceptional, but serves the escalating chaos well.

jokes.text: 'I think everybody has the flu.'
jokes.setup: The bridal party is visibly, catastrophically ill from food poisoning. Everyone knows exactly what's happening.
jokes.punchline: Annie's completely detached, clinical diagnosis — 'I think everybody has the flu' — is a masterpiece of denial and willful misreading of the situation.
jokes.explanation: Six words, perfectly placed. The calm, matter-of-fact delivery amid obvious gastric catastrophe is comic gold. It's pure Annie — unable to accept responsibility, reframing disaster as something mundane and blameless. The economy is near-perfect: maximum absurdity per syllable. This line became genuinely quotable well beyond the film.

jokes.text: 'I need the toilet! I need the toilet!'
jokes.setup: Megan was just claiming her dress was 'probably just tight.' Now the food poisoning hits in full force.
jokes.punchline: The repeated urgent screaming — frantic, undignified — in a high-end bridal boutique is the punchline to her earlier denial.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Megan's denial. It works primarily through escalation and performance energy rather than clever writing, but Melissa McCarthy's commitment makes it land hard with audiences.

jokes.text: The sequence where Megan attempts to use a sink or other non-toilet fixture as a toilet while Annie desperately tries to redirect her ('No! No, Megan. No! No! Look away!')
jokes.setup: There is a bathroom but it is too far. Megan is not going to make it.
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'No! No, Megan. No!' combined with 'Look away!' suggests Megan is doing something deeply inappropriate with bridal boutique fixtures — the audience's imagination is worse than anything shown.
jokes.explanation: Crucially, what's NOT shown is funnier than what could be. The dialogue implies enough — a sink, the instructions to 'look away' — that the audience's imagination does the heavy lifting. The comedy-of-the-unshown is a sophisticated choice that elevates this above pure gross-out.

jokes.text: Helen asks if Annie is okay and whether it was 'that gray kind of lamb' — while Annie is visibly suffering but insisting 'I feel fine.'
jokes.setup: Annie is clearly ill but refusing to admit it, as admitting illness means admitting the restaurant was a bad choice.
jokes.punchline: Helen's sweetly pointed questions ('Was it that? No. I'm... I feel fine') expose the ongoing denial while barely masking her own smugness.
jokes.explanation: Solid but not exceptional character work — the Helen vs. Annie dynamic is well-mined here. The 'gray kind of lamb' is a nice specific detail that grounds the absurdity.

jokes.text: Annie insists she doesn't need to throw up — immediately followed by her throwing up.
jokes.setup: Someone suggests Annie would feel better if she threw up. She firmly: 'I don't have... I don't have to throw up.'
jokes.punchline: The [46:43] timestamp gap strongly implies she immediately vomits, making her denial the setup for an instant physical gag.
jokes.explanation: Classic immediate-denial-reversal structure, executed cleanly. The doubling ('I don't have... I don't have to') adds a nice stammer of uncertainty before the inevitable. Not original but structurally sound.

jokes.text: Annie, to Helen: 'In fact, Helen, I'm hungry. And I wish I had a snack.' — right after everyone is violently ill.
jokes.setup: Annie has just thrown up (or is about to) and is surrounded by food-poisoned bridesmaids. Helen is smugly asking if she's sick.
jokes.punchline: Annie's claim that she's not only fine but STARVING — 'I wish I had a snack' — is a spectacular piece of competitive denial against Helen.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. Annie is so committed to 'winning' against Helen that she overplays her hand — claiming hunger in the middle of a mass vomiting event. 'I wish I had a snack' is the kind of specific, slightly formal phrasing that makes it stick. The escalation from 'I feel fine' to 'I'm starving' is perfect Annie logic. The subsequent Jordan almonds payoff makes this even better.

jokes.text: 'It's coming out of me like lava!'
jokes.setup: The bathroom situation is already catastrophic. Megan is narrating her experience with minimal filter.
jokes.punchline: 'Like lava' — the geological metaphor is so specific and so wrong for the setting that it creates its own comedy.
jokes.explanation: Megan's total lack of decorum and her oddly poetic choice of 'lava' as a comparator is quintessential character comedy. The specificity of the metaphor — not water, not anything mundane, but lava — combined with Melissa McCarthy's delivery makes this one of the most quotable lines in the reel. Pure Megan.

jokes.text: Annie eating Jordan almonds contentedly while everyone around her is violently ill.
jokes.setup: Annie claimed she was hungry and wanted a snack. We expect this to be a bluff.
jokes.punchline: She actually IS eating Jordan almonds — calmly, appreciatively — in the middle of the chaos. 'These are great. Thank you.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. The setup was Annie's absurd denial that she was hungry; the payoff is her literally eating in the chaos. The visual of her calmly munching Jordan almonds — a very specific, bridal-boutique-appropriate snack — while catastrophe unfolds is a brilliant image. The 'These are great. Thank you.' adds a layer of mannered politeness that makes it even funnier.

jokes.text: Annie defending herself: 'I was... I was just hungry.' / 'But it wasn't the restaurant.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is now openly sick from the restaurant Annie chose. Lillian gently confirms it was the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Annie's continued denial — 'But it wasn't the restaurant. No, no, no, no' — in the face of total, overwhelming evidence is now purely absurdist in its commitment.
jokes.explanation: By this point the denial joke is well-established; this is a continuation rather than an escalation. The five 'No's in a row are characterful but the joke has diminishing returns at this stage.

jokes.text: Lillian in her wedding dress, squatting in the street while Annie begs her not to ruin it: 'You're really doing it, aren't you? You're really shitting in the street.'
jokes.setup: Lillian is wearing the stunning two-year-old Lady JuJu wedding dress. She desperately needs a bathroom and can't hold it.
jokes.punchline: Annie's disbelieving, almost admiring commentary — 'You're really shitting in the street' — as Lillian defecates in the gutter while wearing a wedding dress.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of the stunning, expensive, emotionally resonant wedding dress against the brutal indignity of street defecation is the film's central gross-out joke done right. Annie's narration — almost journalistic in its bluntness — adds a layer of bewildered commentary. The repeated 'You're really...' emphasizes the unreality of the moment.

jokes.text: Cut to: 'We'll just take five of the Fritz Bernaises. Thank you, Whitney.'
jokes.setup: We just witnessed a full scene of mass food poisoning, public defecation, and bridal boutique chaos.
jokes.punchline: The immediate cut to Helen calmly placing the dress order as if nothing happened — the original debate about the Fritz Bernaise is resolved by catastrophe.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. The entire dress debate subplot is resolved not by any deliberation but by everyone being too sick to care, and Helen simply closes the transaction. The normalcy of 'Thank you, Whitney' after everything that just happened is a perfect button. Helen winning by default is also sharp character work.

jokes.text: Whitney calmly ordering 'five of the Fritz Bernaises' as the chaos resolves — business as usual
jokes.setup: The entire sequence of food poisoning chaos in the bridal salon has just concluded
jokes.punchline: Whitney pivots immediately to the transaction — 'We'll just take five of the Fritz Bernaises' — as if nothing unusual happened
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the entire set piece. The return to business-as-usual after catastrophe is a classic comedy structure, and 'They really do look better' adds an extra layer of absurdity — the disaster somehow confirmed the salesperson's choice. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'I crapped my wedding dress. I crapped... I... I crapped my wedding dress.'
jokes.setup: Lillian is in the stunning Lady JuJu wedding dress. She just defecated in the street.
jokes.punchline: The stunned, stuttering repetition of 'I crapped my wedding dress' — the broken repetition as the reality sinks in.
jokes.explanation: The repetition is perfect — the stutter of 'I crapped... I... I crapped my wedding dress' captures genuine traumatic processing as comedy. It's funny because it's TRUE and because she can't quite assimilate it. Highly quotable, strong impact. The specificity of 'my wedding dress' rather than just 'in the street' makes it her loss, not just an abstract event.

jokes.text: 'Lunch was fun, though, right? It was a good time, all the girls together.'
jokes.setup: Annie just watched Lillian defecate in a wedding dress in the street after a mass food poisoning event she caused.
jokes.punchline: Annie's breezy reframing of the disaster as a fun lunch outing — 'all the girls together' — is the ultimate denial capping the entire sequence.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke of the entire reel. It is the perfect button to 10+ minutes of escalating chaos. Annie's ability to reframe catastrophic humiliation as 'lunch was fun, though, right?' is both deeply character-specific and genuinely profound comedy. The casualness of 'it was a good time, all the girls together' — as if they'd just had a pleasant brunch — is so committed and so wrong that it becomes a kind of comedic poetry. It's Annie in a nutshell: denial as a coping mechanism deployed with cheerful determination. Earns its exceptional score.

jokes.text: Annie asking to borrow a razor from someone in what appears to be a gas station or convenience store bathroom, clearly shaving her armpit over a sink before a blind date.
jokes.setup: Annie is going on a blind date and is in a dingy public restroom borrowing a stranger's razor.
jokes.punchline: The sheer indignity of the preparation — shaving with a stranger's razor in a gas station — speaks volumes about where Annie is in her life.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual character moment — the pathos of Annie's preparation is funny because it's sad. Using a stranger's razor speaks to her total lack of planning and the low-rent circumstances of her life. The 'Have a good date' from the stranger adds a nice human touch.

jokes.text: Annie tells the stranger 'I'm not over 40' after being asked if her date is also over 40.
jokes.setup: The stranger innocently asks if the guy she's going out with is also over 40, implying Annie looks over 40.
jokes.punchline: Annie's reflexive, slightly wounded 'I'm not over 40. Forget it.' — defending her age while in a gas station bathroom shaving with a stranger's razor.
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional joke that adds pathos to the scene. Annie's pride about her age is funny given her circumstances. The 'Forget it' is a good button.

jokes.text: 'Ow! Sorry.' — Annie waxing/shaving under her arm from a stranger, with a pained reaction.
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to get ready for her date in a public bathroom. The stranger is helping with her arm hair.
jokes.punchline: The 'Ow!' — the casual pain of this undignified preparation.
jokes.explanation: Minor physical beat. Functional — adds to the cringe of the preparation scene — but not particularly inventive on its own.

jokes.text: Tyler: 'Do you watch movies?' — another long pause before Annie can even respond, with the boy staring at her blankly.
jokes.setup: The blind-date setup requires Annie to bond with a child she's never met. Tyler asks the most reductive, conversational question possible.
jokes.punchline: The banality of 'Do you watch movies?' — combined with the visual of the boy staring — implies this is what genuine, unfiltered social awkwardness with a child looks like.
jokes.explanation: Part of the sustained awkward comedy of the Tyler sequence. Works as escalation — each question is weirder than the last.

jokes.text: 'Are you afraid of dying?' / [pause] / 'Because my mom is going to kill you.'
jokes.setup: Tyler asks 'Are you afraid of dying?' — an already disturbing question from a child to a stranger. Annie hesitantly engages with it seriously.
jokes.punchline: 'Because my mom is going to kill you' — the mundane explanation for the existential question. It's both a threat and a deflation.
jokes.explanation: One of the best-structured jokes in the reel. The setup is terrifying enough that Annie (and the audience) has to take it seriously for a moment — 'Are you afraid of dying?' from a blank-faced child is genuinely unsettling. The punchline is simultaneously a relief (oh, it's just a mom warning) and funnier for being so mundane. The economy is extraordinary — 10 words do enormous work. The dark-subversive layer (it IS a kind of death threat) adds texture. Genuinely memorable.

jokes.text: 'Because my mom is going to kill you.' — Tyler's reason for asking if Annie is afraid of dying
jokes.setup: Annie asks Tyler why he asked if she's afraid of dying, expecting a child's existential musing
jokes.punchline: 'Because my mom is going to kill you' — the mundane, petulant child warning his dad's date off
jokes.explanation: Excellent two-beat joke. The setup ('Are you afraid of dying?') seems like a strange philosophical child moment, then the punchline recontextualizes it as a child's protective/possessive threat about his parents. The long pause between setup and payoff (the audience thinks about it for 30 seconds) makes it land harder. Near-perfect economy — seven words deliver the whole joke.

jokes.text: 'You're making me uncomfortable.'
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to make conversation with this child. He has just told her his mom will kill her.
jokes.punchline: Tyler saying Annie is making HIM uncomfortable — reversing who should logically be uncomfortable — is a beautiful inversion.
jokes.explanation: Perfect inversion comedy. Annie is clearly the one who is uncomfortable, so having Tyler declare she's making HIM uncomfortable flips the power dynamic in a funny, unsettling way. The blank delivery makes it land harder.

jokes.text: 'Your hair looks burned.'
jokes.setup: Tyler continues his series of unsettling non-sequitur observations about Annie.
jokes.punchline: A completely unprompted, specific, slightly cruel observation about Annie's hair — 'burned' rather than damaged or frizzy — from a child with no social filter.
jokes.explanation: Part of Tyler's sustained assault on Annie's self-esteem. 'Burned' is a specific, funny word choice — not just 'bad' but actively damaged by fire. The deadpan child delivery elevates it. Contributes to the running gag of the Tyler sequence.

jokes.text: 'Are you going to make a baby with my father?'
jokes.setup: Tyler continues interrogating Annie. He has already established himself as deeply unsettling.
jokes.punchline: The directness of the question — no preamble, no euphemism — delivered with the same flat affect as all his other questions.
jokes.explanation: Classic creepy-child comedy. The blunt directness of the question, in a context where it's the last thing Annie wants to think about, is well-deployed. Part of the Tyler escalation sequence.

jokes.text: 'My grandma died where you're sitting.' / 'She died right here?' / 'Right where your underpants are.'
jokes.setup: Tyler declares his grandma died in that spot. Annie, slightly concerned, asks for clarification.
jokes.punchline: 'Right where your underpants are' — the specificity is both unnecessary and perfectly chosen. Tyler is either genuinely disturbed or running a masterful psychological campaign against Annie.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. The specificity of 'right where your underpants are' escalates from morbid to genuinely bizarre. It's not just 'you're sitting where grandma died' — it's the almost territorial, intimate specificity of 'your underpants.' Whether Tyler is psychologically torturing Annie intentionally or completely innocent, the line works both ways. Highly quotable, earns its score.

jokes.text: 'You wanna watch me dance?' / 'Sure.' — Tyler then dances for an extended beat while Annie watches.
jokes.setup: After the sustained psychological assault, Tyler suddenly pivots to asking Annie to watch him dance.
jokes.punchline: The abrupt tonal shift from creepy interrogation to innocent child wanting to show off a dance — and Annie's resigned 'Sure' — subverts the buildup.
jokes.explanation: The pivot works because it's so sudden. Tyler goes from 'right where your underpants are' to wanting to dance — and Annie's flat 'Sure' captures her complete surrender to the weirdness. The dance itself (inferred from the timestamp gap at 52:05-52:26) is a visual gag payoff.

jokes.text: Annie, mid-dancing with Tyler apparently, suddenly answers her phone in a moment of emotional vulnerability: 'Listen to me. I miss you so much. I'll come over right now. Okay, I'm not over you yet, that's why.'
jokes.setup: Annie is on a blind date — clearly trying to move on. She gets a call, presumably from her ex.
jokes.punchline: In front of a child she just met, she immediately and desperately declares 'I miss you so much. I'll come over right now' — torpedoing the date with complete lack of self-control.
jokes.explanation: Strong character moment — Annie's inability to maintain any boundaries with her ex is funny and sad in equal measure. 'I'm not over you yet, that's why' as an explanation is both pathetic and completely honest. The fact that this is happening in front of Pete's child adds to the cringe.

jokes.text: Annie discovers Pete's son has eaten one of her pills and demands to know which one, then tells him calmly: 'Something's going to happen to you. I don't know what it is, but something's going to happen to your body.'
jokes.setup: Tyler has apparently eaten one of Annie's medications/pills. Annie is horrified.
jokes.punchline: Instead of calling Poison Control or panicking appropriately, Annie issues the vague, ominous warning: 'Something's going to happen to you. I don't know what it is, but something's going to happen to your body.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. The vagueness is what makes it — she can't even be specific about the threat, just 'something... your body.' It's both genuinely alarming as parental irresponsibility and hilarious as an underreaction. The calm, almost confiding delivery ('I don't know what it is') is perfect Annie energy — she's just as lost as everyone else but trying to maintain authority. Quotable and very specific to this character.

jokes.text: 'Did you eat one of those?' / 'I ate Saturday.' — Pete discovering Annie has eaten edibles or similar
jokes.setup: Pete comes back and finds Annie has gotten into something she shouldn't have
jokes.punchline: 'I ate Saturday' — an indeterminate, temporally confused answer suggesting she's already affected
jokes.explanation: 'I ate Saturday' is a genuinely funny, economical line suggesting mild cognitive impairment from whatever she ate. The non-sequitur temporal confusion is a great shorthand for 'this is already affecting her.' Good economy.

jokes.text: 'That was fun. Oh, my gosh.' — Annie after the entire catastrophic blind date interaction with Tyler.
jokes.setup: Annie has just survived a psychologically bruising encounter with Tyler — death threats, underpants, dancing, pill-eating.
jokes.punchline: Her breezy 'That was fun. Oh, my gosh' — the same denial/reframing energy as 'lunch was fun, though, right?'
jokes.explanation: A softer version of the 'lunch was fun' joke. It works because it's Annie's consistent reflex, but it's slightly weaker here because the denial isn't as extreme or as well-timed.

jokes.text: Annie inviting Pete to Lillian's wedding, then immediately walking it back: 'Not like that. Not like anything serious. But just like a fun time.'
jokes.setup: Annie likes Pete but is trying to play it cool and not seem desperate.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate, desperate hedging — 'not like that, not like anything serious, but just like a fun time, we can get dressed up...' — reveals exactly how much she wants him to say yes.
jokes.explanation: Recognizable cringe territory — everyone has watched someone over-explain a casual invitation. Character-specific but not exceptionally written.

jokes.text: Pete declines Annie's wedding invite by saying it would suck for HER to explain their relationship: 'I don't want to make you have to explain to all those people what our relationship is. That would suck for you.'
jokes.setup: Pete is being asked to a wedding by Annie, whom he has a casual arrangement with.
jokes.punchline: He declines by framing his rejection as consideration for HER — a classic maneuver of making a selfish act sound generous.
jokes.explanation: Recognizable relationship humor — the 'I'm doing this for you' rejection is familiar but Pete's breezy delivery makes it land. Annie's quiet 'Yeah. I guess so' is the funnier beat — her internalization of the rejection.

jokes.text: Annie invents a fake date named 'George Glass' to save face — and Pete immediately calls it.
jokes.setup: Stung by Pete's rejection, Annie immediately claims she has someone else to ask — 'this guy, George.'
jokes.punchline: 'George Glass' — the name is so obviously fake, so transparently invented on the spot, that it functions as its own punchline. Pete's calm 'Okay. Who is this George?' makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: 'George Glass' is a perfect fake name — alliterative, slightly too neat, obviously invented. It's also a Brady Bunch reference (Jan's imaginary boyfriend) that adds a meta-layer for audiences who catch it. Annie's subsequent insistence that George is 'very hot, nice' is delicious in its overspecification. The name alone generates most of the comedy.

jokes.text: Pete asks if George Glass 'can do this' — implying sexual activity — followed by an extended beat (54:29-54:42) of implied intimacy.
jokes.setup: Annie has been defending the fictional George Glass as a superior alternative to Pete.
jokes.punchline: Pete's challenge — 'can this George Glass do this to you?' — immediately cuts to a physical beat that presumably makes Annie forget all about George Glass.
jokes.explanation: Functional but predictable. The 'I can do this' physical escalation is a standard move in this type of scene. Annie's 'Probably' — suggesting George could match it — is the better joke within the beat.

jokes.text: 'Probably.' — Annie's answer to whether George Glass could do the same thing to her.
jokes.setup: Pete has just demonstrated something physically impressive/pleasurable, clearly expecting Annie to concede.
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat 'Probably' — refusing to fully capitulate, still nominally defending the fictional George Glass.
jokes.explanation: Perfect one-word joke. The whole sequence has been building toward Annie either capitulating or escalating her George Glass fantasy. 'Probably' is the perfect middle path — she won't admit defeat, but she can't fully commit to the lie either. One word that does complete character work. The delivery timing is everything and the word choice is perfect.

jokes.text: Rhodes (the cop) appears at his patrol car at 5am and asks what brings Annie in so early: 'I've just had a bad night. Boy stuff.' Rhodes: 'Do you want me to arrest anybody? I could do that.'
jokes.setup: Annie shows up clearly distressed. Rhodes, being a cop, asks what's wrong.
jokes.punchline: 'Do you want me to arrest anybody? I could do that.' — using official law enforcement powers as a flirtatious comfort offer.
jokes.explanation: Rhodes is immediately endearing through this line — using his cop powers as a lighthearted comfort offering is a lovely character beat. The 'I could do that' makes it even better by suggesting genuine willingness. Great economy, strong character integration for both Rhodes and the dynamic with Annie.

jokes.text: 'We are just like priests. Except we can tell everybody about it afterwards.' / 'Oh. I won't, though.' / 'Doesn't sound very inviting.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes offers to talk 'like a priest' — implying confidentiality.
jokes.punchline: He undermines this by clarifying that unlike priests, cops can and do tell people everything — then walks it back with 'I won't, though' — which Annie rightly notes is not inviting.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke with a nice structure: setup (we're like priests), reversal (but we tell everyone), secondary reversal (but I won't), and button (Doesn't sound very inviting). The rhythm is good and it's very much in character for Rhodes — charming but slightly hapless.

jokes.text: Rhodes describes his ideal wedding including a carnival with 'people win prizes for guessing the bride's weight,' dunk tanks, and elephants — until Annie notes: 'What you are talking about there, that's a circus wedding. It's a totally different...' / 'Right.' / 'You missed it.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes is trying to be sweet about wanting a stress-free wedding — but his vision escalates from 'carnival' to full circus.
jokes.punchline: Annie's straight-faced correction — 'that's a circus wedding. It's a totally different...' — delivered as genuine advice rather than mockery, is a perfect deadpan beat.
jokes.explanation: The 'bride's weight guessing' is the standout detail — specific, absurd, and slightly dark. The carnival-to-circus escalation is funny, and Annie's taxonomic correction ('that's a circus wedding, it's totally different') plays perfectly against Rhodes's earnestness. 'You missed it' is a lovely button.

jokes.text: Annie corrects Rhodes: 'What you are talking about there, that's a circus wedding. It's a totally different...' / Rhodes: 'Right. You missed it.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes is describing elephants and tightropes as wedding features
jokes.punchline: Annie pedantically distinguishes 'carnival' from 'circus' — then Rhodes's 'You missed it' (you missed the point) adds a playful meta-layer
jokes.explanation: Nice quick beat in the Rhodes/Annie rapport-building. His 'You missed it' is fondly deflating. Good but not standout.

jokes.text: Rhodes presents Annie with an ugly carrot from the bag: 'You got the ugly carrot. There is one in every bag. You have to eat it. It's good luck.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes has been sharing carrots with Annie. She gets an obviously misshapen one.
jokes.punchline: Rhodes's invented mythology of the 'lucky ugly carrot' — delivered with complete sincerity — is charming absurdism.
jokes.explanation: Sweet absurdist moment. The 'one in every bag' and the lucky-ugly-carrot mythology are endearing improvised-feeling character work. The subsequent throwing/littering beat adds physical comedy.

jokes.text: Annie throws the ugly carrot away. Rhodes threatens to fine her for littering. Annie immediately picks it up: 'I'm sorry. It's just that I'm anal about that kind of thing.'
jokes.setup: Annie litters, Rhodes threatens a fine. She picks it up and apologizes.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm anal about that kind of thing' — she JUST littered, making this self-assessment completely wrong in a funny way.
jokes.explanation: Annie's self-contradiction — describing herself as anal about littering immediately after littering — is a nice character beat. The word 'anal' in a flirtatious context also has a mild double-meaning payoff. Good economy.

jokes.text: Annie tells Rhodes she didn't know you could be a cop there if you weren't a citizen — leading to Rhodes's response that they made a 'special dispensation because I'm so tough and strong' — and then, as an afterthought: 'And handsome.'
jokes.setup: Annie queries Rhodes's immigration status as a police officer.
jokes.punchline: Rhodes's list of qualifications — 'tough and strong' — and then, almost shyly, the afterthought 'And handsome' as if this is an official criterion.
jokes.explanation: The afterthought structure — tacking 'handsome' onto 'tough and strong' as an official qualification — is very Rhodes. The timing of the afterthought beat is crucial to the comedy. Nicely self-deprecating/self-aggrandizing simultaneously.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry. It's just that I'm anal about that kind of thing.' — Annie about littering
jokes.setup: Annie throws the carrot away and explains she's particular about cleanliness
jokes.punchline: 'I'm anal about that kind of thing' — inadvertently callback to the food poisoning sequence where 'anal' has a very recent, very specific meaning
jokes.explanation: Whether intentional or not, 'I'm anal about that kind of thing' landing just 10 minutes after the food poisoning disaster sequence is a nice inadvertent callback/double meaning. The rewatch audience will get extra mileage from this.

jokes.text: Annie and Rhodes argue about whether she could be a cop, with Annie saying 'I could be a cop' — and Rhodes's incredulous but playful 'No.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes has been emphasizing his toughness. Annie, feeling competitive, claims she could be a cop.
jokes.punchline: Given everything we've seen Annie do in this reel (food poisoning her bridal party, shaving in a gas station, almost running from a blind date), her claim to be cop-worthy is perfectly absurd.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the speed gun scene. Functional but not exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Rhodes teaches Annie to use the speed gun, and she lets multiple speeders go because she doesn't want to 'ruin their day': 'People are on their way to work. Why ruin their day?'
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to prove she could be a cop by operating the speed gun.
jokes.punchline: She lets speeders go — a 63mph in a presumably 55mph zone — because she empathizes with commuters too much to ticket them.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Annie logic — she's not a bad person, just completely wrong for law enforcement. 'Why ruin their day?' as an anti-cop philosophy is both funny and reveals real character — Annie is empathetic to a fault. Solid character-integrated comedy.

jokes.text: Annie keeps letting speeders off: 'Okay, they were all right. We'll let them go.' / 'People are on their way to work. Why ruin their day?'
jokes.setup: Annie is operating the speed gun and given authority to flag speeders
jokes.punchline: She keeps rationalizing letting everyone go — 'Why ruin their day?' — refusing to enforce the law she was just excited to participate in
jokes.explanation: Annie's conflict-averse, people-pleasing nature transfers hilariously to law enforcement. 'Why ruin their day?' as a law enforcement philosophy is good character comedy. Consistent with Annie's anxious refusal to cause problems for anyone.

jokes.text: Annie apparently clocks a car at 48mph — Rhodes insists it was 48 — Annie is amazed by her own (non-existent) achievement.
jokes.setup: Annie thinks she's being impressive with the speed gun. Rhodes confirms an unlikely reading.
jokes.punchline: The mutual performance of amazement — 'That's never happened. Are you serious? It was 48? I'm so impressed.' — where it's unclear if Rhodes is being sincere or just charming her.
jokes.explanation: Sweet romantic beat. Rhodes either genuinely believes in Annie or is performing belief for her benefit — either reading is charming. Not the sharpest writing but the warmth of the scene carries it.

jokes.text: A car registers 91mph — 'Can we go?' / 'We can go.' / 'Come on, hot dogger.'
jokes.setup: Annie has been letting everyone go. A car doing 91mph finally gets a reaction from both of them.
jokes.punchline: Even at 91 — clearly dangerous — Annie's instinct is 'Can we go?' as if she just witnessed something embarrassing rather than dangerous. Rhodes's 'Come on, hot dogger' is a lovely, slightly archaic term of endearment.
jokes.explanation: 'Hot dogger' is a genuinely charming, funny, slightly old-fashioned term of endearment for Rhodes to deploy. The mutual chase beat — 'Let's get that fucker' — following Annie's moment of letting speeders go is a funny reversal. Good scene button.

jokes.text: 'Let's get that fucker.' — Annie, with full commitment, as they give police chase
jokes.setup: Annie was just releasing everyone going slightly over; now she wants to pursue a 91 mph driver
jokes.punchline: 'Let's get that fucker' — Annie's total reversal, now a zealous law enforcer — delivered with sincere cop-drama commitment
jokes.explanation: Perfect character reversal in four words. The contrast between 'why ruin their day?' moments ago and 'let's get that fucker' is sharp. Annie fully committing to cop-show energy is great. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Annie is on the phone managing bachelorette party calls from multiple people simultaneously — Helen has preemptively called everyone to suggest Vegas, cutting Annie off.
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to plan the bachelorette party — it's her role as maid of honor. She gets a call from Helen about a lake house.
jokes.punchline: Helen has already called everyone and planted the Vegas idea before Annie could organize anything, turning the calls into a succession of people telling Annie what Helen said.
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — the escalating chaos of phone calls where everyone is already pre-sold on Helen's idea before Annie can speak is an efficient comedic expression of their power dynamic. Helen winning by preemptive action is sharp.

jokes.text: Rita's reason for needing Vegas: 'I need a trip that I can fantasize forever so that I am able to have sex with my husband.'
jokes.setup: Rita calls Annie about the bachelorette party destination.
jokes.punchline: Her reason for Vegas is not fun or celebration — it's purely instrumental: she needs fantasy material to maintain intimacy with her husband.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Rita characterization — her marriage is so sexless that she needs to bank Vegas memories to function. Delivered with complete matter-of-factness, which is funnier than if she were embarrassed. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Rita: 'Shut your filthy fucking mouths!' (to her children, mid-phone call) / 'I'm sorry. I'm surrounded by savages.'
jokes.setup: Rita is trying to have a conversation with Annie about the bachelorette party.
jokes.punchline: She interrupts herself to screech at her children and then returns to Annie with elegant understatement: 'I'm surrounded by savages.'
jokes.explanation: Very strong character moment for Rita. The contrast between 'shut your filthy fucking mouths' and the composed return to conversation — 'I'm sorry. I'm surrounded by savages' — is a great comedic gear shift. The word 'savages' as a descriptor for her own children is perfectly Rita. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Rita drops that she 'can get cocaine from my hairdresser' as a seemingly unrelated tangent before hanging up.
jokes.setup: Rita's call is wrapping up. She has already established herself as a trapped, slightly desperate suburban mom.
jokes.punchline: The completely casual mention of a cocaine connection — offered as a Vegas planning resource — delivered with no escalation, as if it's just a practical fact.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The cocaine mention is funny primarily because of its absolute casualness — it's not a confession or a brag, just a resource Rita is offering, like knowing a good caterer. The hairdresser specificity is perfect (of course it's her hairdresser). Complete character economy — this single line tells you everything about Rita's suburban desperation that you need to know.

jokes.text: Becca tells Annie she wants to see Criss Angel 'but I'm scared. Which I sort of love.'
jokes.setup: Becca is enthusiastic about Vegas and specifically about seeing Criss Angel.
jokes.punchline: 'But I'm scared. Which I sort of love.' — the revelation that she's attracted to being scared by a Las Vegas magician is an unexpectedly specific window into Becca's character.
jokes.explanation: Sweet, slightly strange character beat for Becca. 'Which I sort of love' is the right amount of self-awareness. The Criss Angel specificity (a real, slightly déclassé Vegas act) grounds the absurdity.

jokes.text: Megan's bachelorette party pitch: 'Easy-peasy. Vegas it is.' / [Helen has already called her] / 'I want balls in my face.' / 'I love puppets. Balls.' / 'I think it's Vegas.'
jokes.setup: Megan calls to give her bachelorette party input.
jokes.punchline: Megan's sequential non-sequiturs — 'I want balls in my face,' the pivot to 'I love puppets,' and back to 'Balls' — combined with confirming Vegas, creates a stream-of-consciousness comedy burst.
jokes.explanation: Pure Megan. The transition from 'I want balls in my face' to 'I love puppets' and back to 'Balls' is chaotic in the best possible way — Megan is simultaneously coherent (she means Vegas entertainment) and completely unfiltered. The deadpan 'I think it's Vegas' as a closing statement is a good button.

jokes.text: Annie: 'I guess we are undecided.' — after the cascade of calls all saying Vegas.
jokes.setup: Every single person called has said Vegas. The decision is made — by Helen, through everyone else.
jokes.punchline: Annie's completely wrong assessment — 'undecided' — when it's the opposite of undecided, is a last act of denial.
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective callback to Annie's denial theme. Everyone has agreed on Vegas; Annie calling it 'undecided' is her refusing to acknowledge that Helen has already won. Good economy — four words close the sequence.

jokes.text: Annie pesters the man next to her about being an Air Marshal, citing he has no carry-on as evidence
jokes.setup: Annie is nervous on the plane and notices her seatmate has no carry-on luggage
jokes.punchline: She interprets this mundane detail as ironclad proof he is a secret Air Marshal
jokes.explanation: Annie's anxious, conspiratorial logic is perfectly in character — she is so desperate for security that she projects it onto a stranger. The 'no carry-on' detail as proof is a funny, specific piece of deductive nonsense.

jokes.text: 'I'm not an Air Marshal. You don't need to take a watch.' / 'Okay. I've got the first watch.'
jokes.setup: The seatmate flatly denies being an Air Marshal and tells Annie not to take a watch
jokes.punchline: Annie immediately says she has the first watch anyway, completely ignoring him
jokes.explanation: The joke is perfectly structured: denial, acknowledgment, immediate contradiction. The economy is exceptional — four short lines deliver a complete comic beat. Annie's compulsive need for safety overrides all logic, and the deadpan seatmate reaction amplifies it. One of the sharper structural jokes in this reel.

jokes.text: "I've got the first watch" repeated after a second denial
jokes.setup: The man repeats he is not an Air Marshal and doesn't need a watch
jokes.punchline: Annie says "Okay" then immediately repeats "I've got the first watch" — the denial loop is unbreakable
jokes.explanation: The 'Okay… I've got the first watch' beat is a textbook rule-of-three escalation landing on the second beat perfectly. The brief 'Okay' giving false hope of resolution before the repetition is structurally tight.

jokes.text: Annie tells her seatmate she had a dream last night that the plane went down — and he was in it
jokes.setup: Annie is rambling about being a bad flyer to a stranger
jokes.punchline: She reveals he was in her death dream — a deeply overfamiliar, creepy disclosure to a person she just met
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Annie's social obliviousness — the detail 'you were in it' transforms a mundane anxiety disclosure into an accidentally threatening overshare. Classic cringe comedy escalation.

jokes.text: Helen says there is 'much more sense of community in coach' to reassure Lillian about Annie sitting in the back
jokes.setup: Lillian feels guilty that Annie is stuck in coach while they're in first class
jokes.punchline: Helen delivers a transparently false platitude about coach with complete poise, revealing she has never sat in coach and doesn't care
jokes.explanation: Helen's oblivious privilege is her defining trait, and this line crystallizes it. The joke works because it's delivered with sincerity — she genuinely believes it, which makes her more monstrous and funnier than if she were winking at her own callousness.

jokes.text: 'I can't believe you've never been with anybody else.' / 'Just Kevin.'
jokes.setup: Helen and Becca are having an intimate first-class conversation
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Becca has only ever been with one person — delivered with quiet resignation — lands as both sad and funny, with Helen's horror adding the comic framing
jokes.explanation: Economy is the strength here — 'Just Kevin' is a perfectly bleak two-word punchline. The joke sets up the Becca sex comedy thread that escalates through the reel.

jokes.text: Annie, mid-flight anxiety, interrupts the Helen/Becca conversation by asking where the Air Marshal keeps his gun — specifically 'between the cheeks?'
jokes.setup: Annie has been fixated on the Air Marshal theory; she interrupts a private conversation
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'ankle, hip, lower back' to 'between the cheeks' is a sudden, absurd leap that shocks
jokes.explanation: The escalating anatomical specificity — ending on the most transgressive option — is a classic escalation joke. Annie's anxiety has now curdled into obsessive fixation, and the seatmate's flat 'No, I don't stick a gun up my butt. That's stupid.' is a perfect straight-man reply.

jokes.text: 'I didn't say up.' — Annie's clarification about where the gun would go
jokes.setup: The seatmate protests that people don't put guns 'up their asses'
jokes.punchline: Annie pedantically corrects the direction, implying the gun would be held between the cheeks from the outside — a distinction that is somehow worse
jokes.explanation: Three words do an extraordinary amount of comedic work. The joke operates on multiple levels: it's a pedantic correction that makes the original idea somehow more absurd; it reveals Annie has thought about this in granular anatomical detail; and the seatmate's subsequent baffled explanation about the tape marks shows he's now been sucked into her logic. Near the 8.0 anchor in economy and character integration — only Annie, with her runaway anxious brain, would split this particular hair.

jokes.text: The seatmate describes an undercover cop with 'tape marks all up and down his cheeks' as evidence for the butt-gun theory
jokes.setup: He is trying to refute Annie's butt-gun idea but accidentally corroborates a version of it
jokes.punchline: The tape-marks detail is so specific and strange that it becomes funnier than the original premise — he has inadvertently validated her
jokes.explanation: The seatmate breaking his cool to provide supporting evidence for Annie's lunacy is a great reversal. His specific detail — tape marks, plural, 'all up and down' — suggests he has thought about this more than he should have, which is its own joke.

jokes.text: The seatmate offers to demonstrate by cutting a hole in his pocket and hiding his iPod Nano to prove you can retrieve something from between your cheeks
jokes.setup: He is arguing the logistics of a butt-holstered gun
jokes.punchline: He volunteers to physically simulate the retrieval on an airplane, using a Nano, requiring scissors — the commitment to the bit has escalated to pure absurdism
jokes.explanation: The escalation of this bit reaches its peak here. What started as Annie's paranoid fantasy has somehow become the seatmate's passionate science experiment. The absurdity is fully earned by the buildup.

jokes.text: Becca reveals Kevin can only have sex in bed, in the dark, under the covers, only after they've showered — separately — and sometimes he's too tired by the time they finish cleaning
jokes.setup: Helen has expressed pity for Becca having only been with one man
jokes.punchline: Each additional constraint on Kevin's sex requirements is worse than the last; the final reveal that the cleaning ritual defeats him is the peak
jokes.explanation: This is the reel's best sustained joke. The escalating specificity of Kevin's requirements (bed → dark → covers → separate showers → too tired) each lands as its own beat, with Becca's matter-of-fact delivery making it funnier. The final 'I'm not tired. I'm not tired. I'm not tired.' repetition is a character-comedy masterstroke — her barely suppressed desperation bleeding through. Comparable to the vasectomy escalation in the anchor examples; slightly below that threshold because Becca is a supporting character and this world is less established.

jokes.text: Helen tells Becca 'that's why every girl needs those slutty college years' with the confidence of a lifestyle guru
jokes.setup: Helen has been pitying Becca's limited sexual experience
jokes.punchline: Helen's unsolicited, breezy advice about 'slutty college years' as a universal rite of passage is delivered with the absolute authority of someone who clearly had them
jokes.explanation: Helen is at her funniest when she dispenses life advice as though she is a magazine column. 'Slutty college years' as essential self-actualization is a good line with strong quotability. Character-specific without being inscrutable.

jokes.text: Annie wanders into first class mid-Becca conversation and asks for 'a glass of alcohol when you get a chance'
jokes.setup: The serious, intimate Helen-Becca conversation is interrupted
jokes.punchline: Annie's vague, desperate drink order ('a glass of alcohol') signals she has heard nothing and needs everything immediately — the juxtaposition with the delicate emotional conversation is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'A glass of alcohol' as a category rather than a drink is a small, perfectly calibrated expression of Annie's barely-held-together state. Functional, in-character, modest.

jokes.text: Becca's warning that a woman was sucked into the airplane toilet keeps her from going to the bathroom
jokes.setup: Becca needs to use the bathroom
jokes.punchline: She refuses because of an urban legend about toilet suction — delivered with absolute sincerity by someone who clearly believes this happened
jokes.explanation: A quick, competent gag that deepens Becca's character as someone whose world is controlled by unfounded anxieties. Not exceptional but it fits the rhythm of the scene.

jokes.text: Helen offers Annie her scotch to 'kick' the pill, adding 'I'm much smaller than you, so you'll handle it' — visual: Helen is clearly petite
jokes.setup: Helen gave Annie a pill to calm her flying anxiety; Annie says it didn't work
jokes.punchline: Helen's casually poisonous logic — 'I do it all the time, and I'm smaller, so you'll be fine' — is both obviously flawed and perfectly in character for someone accustomed to being right
jokes.explanation: The rewatch value is high because knowing what happens next, Helen's breezy pharmacological advice is even more sinister-funny. 'I'm much smaller than you' as reassurance when you're giving someone drugs and alcohol is gleefully irresponsible.

jokes.text: Helen urging Annie to 'just toss it back, don't waste any more time' as Annie sips the scotch tentatively
jokes.setup: Annie is hesitantly drinking the scotch Helen gave her
jokes.punchline: Helen's impatient coaching — 'toss it back' — frames her as a drug dealer rushing a reluctant customer, amplifying her culpability in what's about to happen
jokes.explanation: More of a beat than a standalone joke, but it's a beat with strong comedic function — Helen's urgency implicates her even more in Annie's coming breakdown.

jokes.text: "Ohh. Look at that. Okay, that'll do it. That'll do it."
jokes.setup: Annie tosses back the full scotch
jokes.punchline: Helen's reaction — "that'll do it" repeated — is both satisfied and vaguely villainous, like someone whose trap just sprung
jokes.explanation: "That'll do it" has a Bugs Bunny dropping an anvil quality — Helen has set something in motion. The repetition underscores it. Modest but pointed character beat.

jokes.text: Becca's sex revelation continues: 'He hasn't kissed me in five years.' 'What are you doing when you are having sex, then?' 'Thinking about other things and wishing it would stop.'
jokes.setup: Helen and Becca's conversation about Kevin continues; Becca has been downplaying how bad things are
jokes.punchline: 'Thinking about other things and wishing it would stop' is an explosively honest admission delivered with complete resignation
jokes.explanation: This is one of the funniest lines in the reel. The setup question is perfect — 'What are you doing when you are having sex, then?' is a genuinely logical response to 'he hasn't kissed me in five years' — and the punchline answer is bleakly hilarious in its candor and economy. 'Wishing it would stop' is the kind of line that gets quoted. Becca's deadpan delivery of her own marital horror elevates this. High quotability, strong craft.

jokes.text: 'Sometimes I just want to watch The Daily Show without him entering me.'
jokes.setup: Becca has been confessing the awfulness of her sex life
jokes.punchline: The specific, mundane detail of The Daily Show makes the complaint both funnier and more pathetic — it's not an exotic or romantic desire she's being denied, just basic cable viewing without unwanted intercourse
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in this reel, possibly the most quotable line in the film. The specificity of 'The Daily Show' is genius — not just 'watch TV,' not 'read a book,' but a specific, slightly intellectual, 30-minute news program. The clinical phrase 'without him entering me' alongside a cable news show creates a collision of registers that is perfect comedy. This is comparable to the highest-tier anchor examples in terms of economy and originality. The joke has legs far beyond the scene.

jokes.text: Annie wanders back into first class visibly high/drunk, announcing 'I'm so much more relaxed. I feel like I'm excited and I feel relaxed and I'm ready to party with the best of them!'
jokes.setup: Helen gave Annie a pill + scotch; we now see the result as she reappears transformed
jokes.punchline: The contrast between Annie's earlier anxious, wound-up state and her now blissfully unhinged calm is the payoff — she's exactly the wrong kind of okay
jokes.explanation: The physical transformation sells this. Wiig's performance here — the loose, happy swagger into first class — is the real joke, and the transcript captures it in the rhythm of her lines. 'Ready to party with the best of them' suggests a person whose filter has fully dissolved.

jokes.text: 'And I'm going to go down to the river' — Annie's drugged non-sequitur
jokes.setup: Annie is rambling happily in first class after being chemically liberated
jokes.punchline: The sudden, unexplained announcement that she's 'going to go down to the river' makes no contextual sense at all — a perfect window into a dissolved mind
jokes.explanation: Four words that are funnier than they have any right to be. The utter non-sequitur of going down to the river — on a plane — delivered with sincere intention is a perfect peak of Wiig's physical comedy.

jokes.text: Helen watching drugged Annie and remarking, 'Wow, it looks like somebody is really relaxing now' with a perfectly composed smile
jokes.setup: Helen has just watched Annie spiral into incoherence from the drugs she provided
jokes.punchline: Her comment is the understatement of the century, delivered with no guilt whatsoever — framing a pharmacological disaster as a successful spa treatment
jokes.explanation: Helen at her most purely comic: surveying the chaos she caused and finding it satisfying. Her character integration is very high here — only Helen could look at a person she just incapacitated and say 'relaxing' with genuine approval.

jokes.text: Annie, drugged, dismisses Helen's restaurant name-drop with 'Big whoop' and suggests they all 'go take a nap'
jokes.setup: Helen is making plans, flexing her social connections
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat 'Big whoop' is the most honest response anyone has ever given Helen, made funnier because it comes from someone who is barely conscious
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: it's funny as a drug-addled response, but it's also the truth — Annie's unfiltered contempt for Helen's social posturing finally has an outlet.

jokes.text: Annie tells the flight attendant trying to remove her: 'Hello, grandpa' and argues 'This is a very strict plane that I'm on'
jokes.setup: A flight attendant is trying to enforce the first-class/coach rule
jokes.punchline: 'Hello, grandpa' as a greeting for an authority figure, followed by classifying the plane's strictness as though reviewing a restaurant, is pure drugged stream of consciousness
jokes.explanation: 'This is a very strict plane' as a complaint is a good, specific absurdist line — Annie has separated herself entirely from the norms of the situation.

jokes.text: Annie tells the flight attendant 'Welcome to Germany. Auf Wiedersehen, asshole.'
jokes.setup: Being escorted out of first class by an authoritative flight attendant
jokes.punchline: The random German farewell is both a non-sequitur and a surprisingly cutting send-off — 'asshole' landing harder after the formal German preamble
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the reel. The 'Welcome to Germany' has no logical explanation, which makes it funnier; 'Auf Wiedersehen, asshole' is the collision of formal and profane that creates a genuinely surprising, quotable moment. The randomness feels earned because Annie's brain is clearly operating in its own dimension.

jokes.text: "Welcome to Germany. Auf Wiedersehen, asshole."
jokes.setup: The flight attendant is forcibly returning Annie to coach and she's resisting
jokes.punchline: Annie's farewell combines a fake German greeting with profanity — completely disconnected from any logic, pure pharmaceutical stream of consciousness
jokes.explanation: "Auf Wiedersehen, asshole" is a banger. The juxtaposition of formal German farewell with casual profanity is exactly the kind of absurdist non-sequitur that gets quoted. Perfect economy, completely unpredictable. One of Wiig's best line readings in the film.

jokes.text: Annie's exit line from first class: 'Catch you on the flip side, motherfuckers.'
jokes.setup: Being forced to return to coach after her first-class rampage
jokes.punchline: A cheerful, gangster farewell — delivered with warmth rather than aggression — is the perfect capper to Annie's first-class visit
jokes.explanation: 'Motherfuckers' as a term of endearment for the first-class cabin she's being expelled from is funny because of its incongruity and because Annie means it affectionately. High quotability and a strong closer to this sequence.

jokes.text: Annie's parting shot: 'This should be open, because it's civil rights. This is the '90s.' / 'You are in the wrong decade.' / 'You are. Okay, I am.'
jokes.setup: Being pushed back toward coach through the curtain
jokes.punchline: Annie invokes civil rights and the 1990s to argue against the first-class curtain, then immediately accepts the correction that she's in the wrong decade — a beat that reveals her brain is fully offline
jokes.explanation: The immediate self-correction 'You are. Okay, I am.' is the best part — the speed at which Annie abandons her civil-rights argument when corrected is perfect. Her brain is so scrambled she can't hold a position for two seconds.

jokes.text: Helen's horrified 'Holy shit. What did you give her?' to Lillian
jokes.setup: Annie has just finished her first-class rampage, which Helen partially engineered
jokes.punchline: Helen asking what Annie was given as though she is an innocent bystander — when she provided the drugs — is a perfect moment of self-serving amnesia
jokes.explanation: The rewatch value is very high because on first viewing it lands as a genuine reaction; on rewatch, knowing Helen provided the drugs herself, her horrified question is a masterpiece of unconscious self-exculpation. Great character moment.

jokes.text: Annie returns in disguise — sunglasses — claiming to be 'Mrs. Iglesias' and insisting she is 'with him' (the seatmate)
jokes.setup: Annie has just been expelled from first class; she attempts to return
jokes.punchline: Her disguise is literally just sunglasses; the flight attendant immediately identifies her ('you were just out here and you put sunglasses on'). The fakeness of the gambit is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A classic comedy gambit — the transparent disguise — but executed with strong character integration. 'Mrs. Iglesias' as her assumed identity is a funny random choice. The seatmate's baffled response (not denying he knows her) adds another layer.

jokes.text: Helen offers Annie her seat so 'Annie shouldn't miss out just because she can't afford it' — said in front of Annie
jokes.setup: Helen is trying to help resolve the standoff
jokes.punchline: Helen's generosity is framed in a way that loudly announces Annie's poverty, which undermines the charity entirely — a perfectly passive-aggressive act of kindness
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Helen's character: the offer is genuine but the phrasing ensures maximum humiliation for Annie. 'Just because she can't afford it' said in front of Annie and a flight attendant is obliviously cruel. High character integration — this is exactly who Helen is.

jokes.text: Annie argues with the flight attendant Steve: 'You can't get anywhere in three seconds.' / 'Well, you'd better try.' / 'You are setting me up for a loss already.'
jokes.setup: Steve gives Annie three seconds to return to her seat
jokes.punchline: 'You are setting me up for a loss already' is a genuinely clever complaint — Annie recognizes the unfairness of the ultimatum but can't do anything about it
jokes.explanation: Annie's protest has the internal logic of a child arguing with a referee, but 'setting me up for a loss' is a surprisingly sharp observation. The specificity makes it funnier than a generic complaint.

jokes.text: 'Whatever you say, Stove.' / 'It's Steve.' / 'Stove. What kind of name is that? That's not a name. My name is Steve. Are you an appliance?' / 'No, I'm a man, and my name is Steve.' / 'You are a flight attendant.' / 'That's absolutely accurate.'
jokes.setup: Annie mispronounces the flight attendant's name as 'Stove'
jokes.punchline: The exchange spirals: Steve's indignant correction leads to Annie's existential challenge ('are you an appliance?'), and his deadpan final answer — 'That's absolutely accurate' to being called a flight attendant — is a perfect straight-man landing
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's standout extended exchanges. 'Stove' as a mispronunciation is funny; the extended riff where Annie interrogates Steve's humanity ('are you an appliance?') elevates it to something genuinely clever. Steve's dignified 'That's absolutely accurate' to 'you are a flight attendant' — accepting the diminution without complaint — is the perfect deadpan cap. Well-structured back-and-forth.

jokes.text: Annie propositions the seatmate ('not-Air Marshal Jon') to 'get back in that restroom and not rest'
jokes.setup: Annie, now fully high and confident, encounters her seatmate in the aisle
jokes.punchline: Annie's clumsy euphemism for sex is both transparently obvious and weirdly charming — she's flirting with the man she's been treating as her bodyguard all flight
jokes.explanation: A reasonable payoff to the Air Marshal running gag — Annie's disinhibited flirtation with a stranger she just met is consistent and funny. The phrasing is a bit limp compared to the reel's best lines.

jokes.text: Annie leans over the seatmate, he describes heat from his 'undercarriage,' she is visibly trapped and he is leering — physical comedy of Annie stuck in a compromising position
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to get back to her seat; the man traps her with his leg
jokes.punchline: His 'steam heat from my undercarriage' line, combined with the visual of Annie pinned in the aisle, is a good physical cringe beat
jokes.explanation: Physical gag that relies primarily on performance. 'Undercarriage' is a reasonable euphemism choice but the moment is more of a setup for Annie's predicament than a joke with a strong punchline of its own.

jokes.text: "Somebody found a souvenir. You feel that steam heat coming? That's from my undercarriage."
jokes.setup: Annie has brushed against or encountered her neighbor's leg/body while trying to return to her seat
jokes.punchline: He calls it a "souvenir" and references "steam heat from my undercarriage" — aggressively oversharing with bizarre confidence
jokes.explanation: "That's from my undercarriage" is a memorably weird line — clinical yet gross, suggesting a character with zero social calibration. Cringe-funny.

jokes.text: Annie, drugged, tells someone 'I don't want you to be a big fuck-up like me' and 'You are more beautiful than Cinderella. You smell like pine needles and you have a face like sunshine.'
jokes.setup: Annie is wandering around the plane, now fully incapacitated, and encounters various passengers
jokes.punchline: The Cinderella compliment is delivered with religious sincerity and is so over-the-top specific ('pine needles') that it's a perfect expression of Annie's scrambled affectionate brain
jokes.explanation: 'You smell like pine needles and you have a face like sunshine' is a highly quotable, specifically absurd compliment that could only come from Annie in this state. 'More beautiful than Cinderella' as an opening gambit is funny on its own; the specific sensory follow-ups make it memorable. High quotability.

jokes.text: Annie announces there is 'a Colonial woman on the wing — she was churning butter' and demands Steve go get her
jokes.setup: Turbulence hits; Annie is in full drug-and-alcohol psychosis on a plane
jokes.punchline: The Colonial woman on the wing is a classic Twilight Zone reference recontextualized through Annie's scrambled brain — the butter-churning specificity elevates it from simple hallucination to its own absurd world
jokes.explanation: A legitimately clever joke. The Twilight Zone allusion (man on the wing) filtered through Annie's historical confusion creates something new. 'Churning butter' is the detail that makes it — it's not just a woman, it's a woman engaged in period-accurate domestic labor. The subsequent panic — 'She is out there right now. Shit!' — escalates it into full comic chaos.

jokes.text: Annie's seatmate springs up claiming to be an Air Marshal — 'I'm an Air Marshal! I've got your back, Jon!'
jokes.setup: Annie's plane chaos has reached peak pandemonium; someone needs to claim authority
jokes.punchline: The seatmate who spent the entire flight denying being an Air Marshal now dramatically reveals himself as one — a perfect callback payoff
jokes.explanation: The best structural joke of the reel. The entire Air Marshal setup — Annie's paranoid theory, his repeated denials, her stubborn insistence — was a 10-minute investment that pays off in one line. He was an Air Marshal the whole time. Annie was right. The payoff earns its 9.0 structure score because it's a perfect long-form callback: the audience's delight is multiplied by the memory of every denial. Annie's 'Yes! I knew it. I got your back, Jon!' completes it. Near-exceptional craft for a running-gag resolution.

jokes.text: "Yes! I knew it. I got your back, Jon!"
jokes.setup: Jon reveals himself as an Air Marshal
jokes.punchline: Annie's triumphant vindication — "I knew it. I got your back, Jon!" — delivered as if she has been his professional partner all along, using his name casually
jokes.explanation: "I got your back, Jon" completes the arc: Annie has been treating him as her Air Marshal partner since minute one, and now she gets to be right. The use of his first name as if they're colleagues is the perfect button. This and joke 40 together form one of the film's best comedy sequences.

jokes.text: 'Who is she? What does she want?' — Annie's last plaintive question about the Colonial woman
jokes.setup: The plane chaos is calming down; Annie is still fixated on the hallucination
jokes.punchline: The question treats the Colonial woman as a real, motivated person with a specific agenda — Annie's concern is genuine, which is what makes it funny
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective capper to the Colonial woman bit. Annie's earnest concern for the wing-woman's motivations is a lovely absurdist beat that shows how deep into the hallucination she has gone.

jokes.text: Lillian tells Annie she is 'starting to make you crazy' and that Helen 'just knows how to do this kind of stuff' — the conversation where Lillian fires Annie from planning duties
jokes.setup: Annie expects to reconcile after the plane incident; Lillian is about to remove her from shower planning
jokes.punchline: The cringe here is sustained and uncomfortable — Lillian is being gentle but each euphemism ('flow smoothly,' 'she's good at it') is a fresh wound. It's not a laugh-out-loud joke but a sustained comedic discomfort that the audience recognizes as the film's central tension crystallized
jokes.explanation: More dramatic than comedic, but the sustained discomfort functions as cringe comedy. Lillian's gentle firing of Annie is funny-painful rather than funny-funny. Included as a comedic moment because the audience squirms; scored modestly because the craft is in the drama, not the joke writing.

jokes.text: 'You don't have to plan any more lunches or trips... You don't have to do anything you don't want to do.'
jokes.setup: Lillian is explaining why she's handing everything to Helen — framed as liberation
jokes.punchline: The 'liberation' rhetoric precisely describes the things Annie valued most and was proud to do — the cruelty of presenting demolition as a gift
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy of manners — this is funny in the way a knife is funny. The irony is there but the scene is playing predominantly for drama. Scored conservatively.

jokes.text: 'I feel like her life is going off and getting perfect, and mine is just like...' [trails off with a vague gesture]
jokes.setup: Annie is venting to Rhodes about her friendship with Lillian and her own life
jokes.punchline: The trailing off — 'mine is just like...' with no completion — the absence of words being funnier than any word she could have chosen
jokes.explanation: Annie's inability to even articulate her own disaster is the joke. The trailing gesture is perfectly economical — the audience fills in everything she can't say.

jokes.text: Rhodes saying if he weren't a cop he would 'go out with a gun and shoot people' — then immediately correcting himself: 'I probably wouldn't do that. I'm just trying to make you feel better.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes is trying to make an analogy about doing what you love regardless of financial failure
jokes.punchline: The analogy breaks down spectacularly when he reaches the violent implication; his immediate self-correction is funnier than the original slip
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. The analogy failing so catastrophically — a cop's passion project would logically be shooting people — and his genuine bafflement at his own phrasing ('I probably wouldn't do that') is a sharply crafted beat. Only a cop character could make this joke, and the structure — confident analogy → catastrophic realization → sheepish correction — is well-executed.

jokes.text: Rhodes, mid-getting-to-know-you conversation, declares 'I hate buttons' as a non-sequitur
jokes.setup: Rhodes has been earnestly trying to connect with Annie
jokes.punchline: The sudden, apparently heartfelt confession about hating buttons — with no context or follow-up — is a deliberately odd beat of character revelation that suggests real quirk rather than romantic-comedy smoothness
jokes.explanation: Three words delivered at the right moment. 'I hate buttons' works because it's such a mundane, unexplained confession dropped into an intimate scene — it feels genuine, which makes it funnier than a bigger joke would be. The economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Rhodes apologizes for the mountain bike in the bedroom — 'Sorry, it's a mountain bike. Are you okay? Do you like mountain biking?'
jokes.setup: Annie and Rhodes are heading to the bedroom; there is apparently a large mountain bike in it
jokes.punchline: The apologetic mid-seduction acknowledgment of a mountain bike in the bedroom, followed by the pivot to 'do you like mountain biking?' as a conversational gambit, is endearingly awkward
jokes.explanation: A good visual-gag-via-dialogue moment. The mountain bike in the bedroom humanizes Rhodes and defuses the romantic tension in a funny, specific way. His attempt to recover the moment with 'do you like mountain biking?' is a nicely awkward pivot.

jokes.text: Rhodes and Annie exchange 'It was fun / It was very fun / I had fun / It was fun' in increasingly stilted morning-after small talk
jokes.setup: Morning after their night together; both are navigating awkwardness
jokes.punchline: The repetition of 'fun' escalates from warm to desperate to comic — the word is drained of all meaning by the fourth usage while both characters smile through it
jokes.explanation: Effective comedic use of repetition and awkward silence. The joke is structural — the same word used four times — and the audience recognizes the social agony of post-sex small talk. Well-observed.

jokes.text: Rhodes offers 'a different kind of fun' as a coded second-round invitation — 'if you care to accompany me to the kitchen, the fun may continue. A different kind of fun.'
jokes.setup: Morning after; Rhodes is trying to extend the encounter
jokes.punchline: His overly formal phrasing for 'want to do it again?' — 'if you care to accompany me' — is funny because it's such an incongruously polite request after the intimacy they've already shared
jokes.explanation: A pleasant, modest joke. The formal register applied to an informal situation is a reliable comic structure. Not exceptional but appropriate and well-timed.

jokes.text: "If you care to accompany me to the kitchen, the fun may continue. A different kind of fun."
jokes.setup: Post-sex morning awkwardness; both have been saying "fun" repeatedly
jokes.punchline: Rhodes uses the word "fun" a fifth and sixth time but distinguishes it as "a different kind of fun" — both a callback to the "fun" loop and an awkward quasi-flirtation about breakfast vs. sex
jokes.explanation: Extends the "fun" running gag one beat further. The formal phrasing "if you care to accompany me" is charmingly awkward. Modest laugh.

jokes.text: Rhodes has secretly gone out and bought baking supplies to encourage Annie to bake — 'I popped out and got a few little baking bits and pieces'
jokes.setup: Rhodes learned Annie used to be a baker; he wants to encourage her
jokes.punchline: The sweet gesture is immediately also a cringe moment — he has overstepped, gone through her private conversation, and is now projecting a fix. The audience simultaneously appreciates and dreads this.
jokes.explanation: More of a dramatic-comedy beat than a pure joke, but the cringe of a man going grocery shopping at dawn to fix a woman he just met functions as dark comedy of good intentions. Modest score reflects that it's primarily plot.

jokes.text: Annie's voicemail to Lillian: 'The excitement still continues with me. I just slept with a cop that pulled me over and I woke up today, and he was really sweet and nice and cute. So, naturally, I ran out as fast as I could.'
jokes.setup: Annie is leaving Lillian a voicemail update on her life
jokes.punchline: 'So, naturally, I ran out as fast as I could' — the self-aware confession that she sabotaged a good thing the moment she recognized it is Annie's character flaw made explicit and comic
jokes.explanation: 'So, naturally, I ran out as fast as I could' is a beautiful line because it's fully self-aware and self-defeating simultaneously. Annie knows exactly what she's doing and finds it as absurd as the audience does. The 'naturally' is the perfect word choice — it acknowledges that this is her pattern, not a one-time mistake. High character integration: this joke is Annie's entire character in seven words.

jokes.text: "I just slept with a cop that pulled me over and I woke up today, and he was really sweet and nice and cute. So, naturally, I ran out as fast as I could. What's wrong with me?"
jokes.setup: Annie is recapping the night to Lillian's voicemail
jokes.punchline: "So, naturally, I ran out as fast as I could" — the word "naturally" doing all the work, acknowledging her own self-destructive pattern with rueful self-awareness
jokes.explanation: "Naturally, I ran out as fast as I could" is a great character line — Annie is fully aware of her own self-sabotage, which makes it funnier and sadder. "What's wrong with me?" asked with genuine bafflement after perfectly describing her own psychology is the right button.

jokes.text: Annie's roommate Brynn announces she got a package, then adds 'I'd bring it to you, but you said, "Don't touch my things."'
jokes.setup: Annie is woken up by her roommate Brynn
jokes.punchline: Brynn withholds the package — which might require attention — because of a rule Annie set, delivered with cheerful passive-aggression or genuine literal-mindedness; either reading is funny
jokes.explanation: Brynn is established as an oddly specific, literal-minded character, and this line captures her perfectly. The logic — 'I could help but you told me not to' — is both maddening and funny. A solid closing beat.

jokes.text: Jewelry store clerk's unprompted, escalating prophecy that Annie's best friend will find someone better — prettier, richer, skinnier — delivered to a customer just trying to buy a necklace
jokes.setup: Annie asks for a 'Best Friends Forever' necklace; clerk questions the word 'forever'
jokes.punchline: The clerk spirals into a weirdly specific, devastating prediction that the friend will find a new, superior best friend and leave Annie behind
jokes.explanation: The clerk's unsolicited, eerily accurate emotional forecast is funny because it mirrors Annie's real anxieties about Lillian and Helen — but delivered as banal retail small talk. The escalation ('prettier and richer and skinnier') turns an uncomfortable observation into a comedic prophecy. It's character-specific to Annie's situation and earns its laughs through escalation rather than shock.

jokes.text: Annie and the teenage jewelry clerk trade increasingly childish insults, culminating in Annie calling her 'a little cunt'
jokes.setup: Annie, an adult woman, gets into a petty argument with a teenage store clerk
jokes.punchline: The insult war escalates to the nuclear option — Annie drops 'you're a little cunt' at a teenage girl in a jewelry store
jokes.explanation: The escalating exchange is well-structured: each comeback is progressively more juvenile, which makes the final atomic bomb of an insult landing on a teenager shocking and hilarious. The jokes along the way ('call me when your boobs come in' / 'you call me when yours come in') are perfectly calibrated tit-for-tat that make Annie's regression visible in real time. The final word earns a huge reaction because it's precisely the wrong thing for an adult to say — and yet completely believable from Annie in her current spiral. The structure alone justifies the high score.

jokes.text: Beat exchange: 'Did you forget to take your Xanax this morning?' / 'God, I feel bad for your parents.' / 'I feel bad for your face.'
jokes.setup: Argument between adult Annie and teenage clerk is heating up
jokes.punchline: 'I feel bad for your face' — a playground-level comeback delivered with full conviction by a grown woman
