jokes.explanation: Each rung of the ladder here is funny on its own. 'I feel bad for your face' is the highlight — maximally childish and maximally quotable. Good economy and character specificity. Part of the larger joke sequence (#2) but distinct enough to call out.

jokes.text: Beat: Annie, after calling a teenager a cunt, quietly says 'I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Annie has just said the worst possible thing to a teenage girl
jokes.punchline: A tiny, almost inaudible 'I'm sorry' — far too small an apology for what just happened
jokes.explanation: The humor is entirely in the gap between the offense and the response. One word, maximum comedy. Perfect economy. The understatement is the joke — she knows she crossed a line and her deflated 'I'm sorry' acknowledges it while also being completely inadequate. Classic Wiig.

jokes.text: Rhodes' voicemail: 'Since you're not returning any of my calls, I assume you're not interested... So don't worry, I won't be bothering you ever again.' Then: 'Get those taillights fixed.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes leaves what sounds like a dignified, restrained breakup voicemail
jokes.punchline: He tags it with an entirely practical, cop-brained reminder about taillights — undercutting all emotional weight he just built
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy. The voicemail is structured as a dignified farewell, and the taillights callback completely deflates the emotional register — but in a way that's completely true to who Rhodes is. Only a good-natured cop who genuinely cares about road safety (and Annie) would do this. It's funny, touching, and character-specific all at once. Scores high because it simultaneously advances plot, deepens character, and delivers a genuine laugh through perfect structural contrast.

jokes.text: Roommates Gil and Brynn deliver eviction notice using corporate HR-speak euphemisms: 'We'd like to invite you to no longer live with us anymore.'
jokes.setup: Annie's bizarre manchild roommates are asking her to move out
jokes.punchline: 'We'd like to invite you to no longer live with us anymore' — framing an eviction as an exclusive invitation
jokes.explanation: The linguistic inversion is clever: an eviction dressed up as a party invitation. Very much in keeping with how these characters talk — politely weird, with slightly formal British affect. 'Invite you to no longer live with us' is a genuinely funny construction.

jokes.text: Gil and Brynn explain their reasoning: it's 'immature' for a grown brother and sister to live together WITH a roommate, so they're going to live together ALONE
jokes.setup: Gil and Brynn say it's immature and 'a bit ridiculous' for a grown brother and sister to still be living together with a roommate
jokes.punchline: Their solution is to continue living together — just without Annie — missing entirely that the sibling cohabitation is the weird part
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Gil and Brynn are completely blind to their own absurdity. They are the weird part of the situation, but they've scapegoated Annie. Their earnest delivery of this upside-down logic is funny precisely because they're convinced of their own reasonableness. Strong character integration — this joke only works with these two specific people.

jokes.text: Gil and Brynn argue over timing of Annie's move: 'She will move.' / 'Eventually.' / 'Eventually.' / 'She has to.'
jokes.setup: Gil and Brynn have just told Annie she has to leave — she's visibly stunned
jokes.punchline: They bicker quietly over whether she'll leave, landing on the noncommittal 'eventually' — as if she might just never go
jokes.explanation: A smaller laugh that extends the roommate scene's absurdism. 'Eventually' as an answer to 'will she move?' lands because they've rendered Annie's departure as uncertain, which reveals just how low the floor of her life is. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Annie stares in stunned silence while Brynn observes: 'She is taking it in.' Then: 'You have to leave.' / 'Oh! That's prickly.'
jokes.setup: Annie is frozen in place, unable to process being evicted by her own bizarre roommates
jokes.punchline: Brynn narrates Annie's internal state like a nature documentary, then Gil's blunt 'You have to leave' is called 'prickly' — an absurdly mild descriptor
jokes.explanation: 'That's prickly' as a response to 'You have to leave' is a nicely weird understatement in Gil/Brynn's specific register. The nature-documentary narration of Annie's paralysis is a solid beat that extends the scene's absurdism.

jokes.text: Annie shows up at her mother's door and says: 'Remember when you thought I hit bottom? That wasn't bottom.'
jokes.setup: Annie's life has been visibly collapsing across the whole film
jokes.punchline: She cheerfully announces that the previous low point was not, in fact, the low point — with casual matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: Economical and quotable. 'That wasn't bottom' is the kind of line that gets used outside of its original context. The delivery — matter-of-fact, almost cheerful — is what makes it land. It encapsulates the film's thesis about Annie's spiral while being genuinely funny. High economy score because it communicates the entire arc of the scene with five words.

jokes.text: Annie's mom responds to rock bottom news by enthusiastically announcing what just came in on Netflix: Cast Away — 'It's like Forrest Gump, but on an island.'
jokes.setup: Annie tells her mom she's hit a new low; this is a mother-daughter crisis moment
jokes.punchline: Mom pivots immediately to Netflix excitement, describing Cast Away with the enthusiasm of someone who has just discovered cinema
jokes.explanation: 'It's like Forrest Gump, but on an island' is a genuinely funny description that works on two levels: it's the kind of summary a loving but oblivious parent would offer, and it's also not entirely wrong. The pivot from crisis to Netflix recommendation is the right length and the right speed. Highly character-specific to this mom.

jokes.text: Annie arrives at Helen's bridal shower to find a valet parking attendant and a full estate; she's directed to 'the stables' and 'the second bridge'
jokes.setup: Annie pulls up to what she expects to be a home — it's an estate with stables and multiple bridges
jokes.punchline: The sheer absurdity of the scale is communicated through Annie being redirected twice just to reach the shower
jokes.explanation: A visual comedy beat that sets up the class-gap tension of the shower scene. Functional rather than exceptional — the joke is the scale of the estate, which the audience sees rather than hears. Gets the job done.

jokes.text: Annie is handed a glass of pink lemonade, says 'Pink lemonade. Nice. Nice touch.' — then immediately: 'Shit.' as she spills it / fumbles without a cup holder
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to be a gracious guest at an intimidatingly upscale party
jokes.punchline: She immediately fumbles the offered drink because her car has no cup holder; her murmured 'Shit' captures her inability to function at this level
jokes.explanation: A small but effective fish-out-of-water beat. Annie's self-narration ('Pink lemonade. Nice. Nice touch.') followed instantly by 'Shit' is good comic rhythm. The cup holder detail is a nice specific touch.

jokes.text: Annie, now inside the party, tastes the pink lemonade and says 'God damn it, that's good. Mmm. Shit, that is fresh.' — in spite of herself
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to be contemptuous of Helen's ostentatious party
jokes.punchline: The lemonade is so good it breaks through her resistance; her profanity-laden compliments betray her
jokes.explanation: 'Shit, that is fresh' as a lemonade review is a funny line — the profanity doing the work of genuine astonishment. It also characterizes Annie perfectly: her resistance crumbling against genuinely excellent party catering is both funny and reveals her complicated feelings about the whole situation.

jokes.text: Guest at the shower declares 'This is the most beautiful shower I have ever been to' and another notes the 'cutest party favors' — pink berets
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to process her surroundings at an absurdly over-the-top bridal shower
jokes.punchline: The guests' rapturous reactions to things like branded pink berets underscore just how over-the-top Helen's production is, playing as comedy through excess
jokes.explanation: Mild world-building comedy. The joke is atmospheric rather than sharp — it establishes the shower's over-the-top quality to set up Annie's later explosion. Not particularly funny on its own.

jokes.text: Annie tells Lillian 'Yeah, I'm here. I was invited. Sorry.' — Lillian says 'Of course you were. I just meant you have arrived.' Annie: 'No, I was just joking. Okay.'
jokes.setup: Annie is defensive and raw at the party; she preemptively justifies her presence
jokes.punchline: Lillian's perfectly innocent response reveals Annie misread the moment entirely; Annie then tries to retroactively claim she was joking
jokes.explanation: A quick cringe moment that shows Annie's anxiety in action — she's primed for conflict and projects it onto a neutral greeting. The quick 'No, I was just joking. Okay.' is a recognizable social fumble. Good character work, minor laugh.

jokes.text: Lillian opens Annie's gift — a handmade scrapbook of Milwaukee memories — and the room genuinely moves
jokes.setup: Helen has been showering Lillian with increasingly expensive and elaborate gifts; Annie's is homemade
jokes.punchline: Annie's low-budget, heartfelt gift lands more emotionally than anything Helen could buy — but Annie is too far gone into her spiral to let herself enjoy it
jokes.explanation: More of a plot beat with comedic texture than a pure joke. The humor comes from the gap between Helen's Paris trip and Annie's Milwaukee scrapbook — both touching and funny in context. Lower scores because the moment is primarily emotional rather than comedic.

jokes.text: Helen says she 'didn't get a chance to actually get a present' because she 'has been so busy organizing the shower' — and hands Lillian a card
jokes.setup: Helen has just thrown a Parisian-level bridal shower at her estate; everyone assumes her gift will be proportionally spectacular
jokes.punchline: She claims she only had time for a card — setting up the Paris reveal as a fake-out
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection setup for the Paris reveal. The understated 'just a card' from someone who built a shower with a second bridge is a solid structural piece. Rewatch bonus because viewers know it's fake-out and appreciate Helen's performance of modesty.

jokes.text: Helen reveals the card says she's taking Lillian to Paris — then triumphantly mocks Lillian's shocked face: 'Your face! I got you! I fooled you!'
jokes.setup: Everyone (including audience) has been primed to think Helen gave just a card
jokes.punchline: The card reveals a Paris trip; Helen's subsequent gloating — 'Look at your face!' — is funnier than the reveal itself
jokes.explanation: Helen's delight in her own trick — 'I got you! I fooled you!' — reveals her competitive nature in a funny way. It's not just a generous gift; she needs to win at gift-giving. That character detail makes it funnier than a straight Paris reveal would be.

jokes.text: Annie whispers 'Are you fucking kidding me?' as Lillian celebrates the Paris gift
jokes.setup: Annie's gift has just been genuinely well-received — and then Helen one-ups it with an entire international trip
jokes.punchline: Annie's barely contained explosion: a barely whispered profanity that signals something bigger is about to detonate
jokes.explanation: A pressure-building beat. The whispered 'Are you fucking kidding me' is funny as the last moment before Annie loses it entirely. It signals the audience that the volcano is about to erupt.

jokes.text: Annie erupts: accuses Helen of stealing her Paris idea, then pivots to: 'What woman gives another woman a trip to Paris? Am I right? Lesbian. We're all thinking it, aren't we?'
jokes.setup: Annie is in full public meltdown, trying to recruit the room to her side
jokes.punchline: 'Lesbian. We're all thinking it, aren't we?' — a transparently bad attempt to win allies by saying the quiet part loud, and it fails spectacularly ('I'm not.' / 'I was.')
jokes.explanation: The punchline gets a split crowd response in the room (immediate denial then 'I was') which is funny both as script and as meta-commentary on audience reactions. Annie's desperate attempt to build consensus by saying something that immediately backfires is peak cringe comedy. The quick 'I was' from one party guest is an underrated punchline within a punchline.

jokes.text: Annie, mid-meltdown, pauses to point out the cookie is too big for the group: 'Did you really think that this group of women was going to finish that cookie? Really?'
jokes.setup: Annie is having a full public breakdown at a bridal shower
jokes.punchline: She interrupts her own emotional spiral to make a completely valid, entirely petty point about cookie portion size
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'you've changed, Lillian' to 'also that cookie is an unrealistic portion' is a beautiful comedic gear shift. The observational point is real (a novelty cookie at a party IS usually too big to finish), and Annie making it in the middle of a breakdown shows how her mind works — she can't stay on the rails even when she's trying to be righteous. This is Annie's character distilled to pure form.

jokes.text: Annie declares she 'never got a chance to try that fucking cookie' and storms off to eat it
jokes.setup: Annie has been raging about the cookie for thirty seconds
jokes.punchline: She interrupts her own outrage speech to go eat the thing she's been complaining about
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation and callback. The audience has been watching the cookie gag build, and the payoff — Annie physically going to get the cookie she's been complaining about — is the best possible resolution. 'I never got a chance to try that fucking cookie' is funny as a line and as an action. It's self-defeating and completely in character.

jokes.text: Annie bites the cookie, then pauses: 'Delicious! Stupid cookie.' Then considers: 'I think I'll dip it in the chocolate.'
jokes.setup: Annie has dramatically stormed over to eat the cookie she's been raging about
jokes.punchline: It's delicious. She admits it. Then she wants to dip it. The cookie wins.
jokes.explanation: 'Delicious! Stupid cookie' is a perfect line. Annie cannot even eat the thing she's using as a protest prop without being won over by it. 'I think I'll dip it in the chocolate' takes it one step further — she's so thoroughly betrayed by her own body that she's actively making the cookie experience better in the middle of a breakdown. This is Annie in a nutshell: her self-sabotage extends even to cookies. High scores across the board because this is fully earned — four jokes building to this moment.

jokes.text: Annie, holding the cookie, dips it in the chocolate fountain and scalds herself: 'All right, let's have some nice, hot, unsanitary chocolate!' then 'Ahh! It's hot! Jesus! God!'
jokes.setup: Annie has decided to dip the cookie in the chocolate fountain despite everything
jokes.punchline: She burns herself immediately — the universe punishes her for the indulgence
jokes.explanation: 'Nice, hot, unsanitary chocolate' is a funny line in itself — Annie calling out the sanitary issues of a chocolate fountain even as she uses it. The burn is deserved comic punishment. Impact is strong because the visual of her scalding herself mid-breakdown is slapstick gold.

jokes.text: Annie, still raging, grabs the chocolate fountain: 'All right, let's have some nice, hot, unsanitary chocolate!'
jokes.setup: Annie has been building toward a physical act of sabotage at the shower
jokes.punchline: 'Unsanitary' is the comedic word choice — she's going to ruin the party by turning the decorative fountain into a weapon, but she's narrating it with weirdly precise food safety consciousness
jokes.explanation: The word 'unsanitary' is doing all the work here — it's an oddly specific, health-inspector register word that makes the chaos feel simultaneously impulsive and weirdly considered. Good comedic word choice.

jokes.text: Helen responds to 'perfectly bleached asshole' insult by confirming it and escalating: 'You know what? It is! And you know how I know? Because I went to the fucking salon with her and I got my asshole bleached, too! And I love my new asshole!'
jokes.setup: Annie hurls 'I'm sure Helen's asshole is perfectly bleached' as an insult designed to embarrass
jokes.punchline: Helen confirms it, one-ups it, invites Lillian along on the trip, and declares love for her new asshole — turning the insult into a brag
jokes.explanation: This is the best line of the reel and among the best in the film. The comedic logic is perfect: Annie fires an insult that she assumes will humiliate Helen; Helen responds by enthusiastically confirming it and bragging about it. 'I love my new asshole!' is an extraordinary line — it's disgusting, escalating, and completely in character for a woman like Helen who would absolutely do this and be proud of it. The audience's gasp-laugh at this response is enormous. The structure is textbook misdirection: the 'obvious' response is denial or embarrassment; instead Helen doubles down. High scores are fully justified.

jokes.text: Lillian, trying to end the fight, says: 'Why can't you just be happy for me and then go home and talk behind my back later, like a normal person?'
jokes.setup: Annie is having a very public meltdown; Lillian is mortified and angry
jokes.punchline: Lillian's request to be gossiped about privately rather than confronted publicly — framed as the reasonable ask — is a funny inversion of normal social values
jokes.explanation: 'Go home and talk behind my back later, like a normal person' is a genuinely quotable inversion. It acknowledges that talking behind someone's back is what actually happens — the ask isn't for honesty, it's for social convention to be maintained. It's also a very real thing people think but never say. High quotability because it works completely out of context.

jokes.text: Helen, after Annie storms out: 'No, no! She does not get a party favor. She does not get a dog!'
jokes.setup: Annie has just caused a spectacular scene and is leaving in disgrace
jokes.punchline: Helen's immediate concern is party favor logistics — specifically that Annie not receive a dog
jokes.explanation: 'She does not get a dog' is a great line because it reveals two things simultaneously: (1) Helen's party favors are live dogs, which is absurdly over-the-top even for her, and (2) Helen's post-fight priority is administrative — making sure Annie gets nothing. 'She does not get a dog' has an almost bureaucratic finality that's very funny. The dogs-as-party-favors detail is itself a visual gag.

jokes.text: Lillian tells Annie not to come to her wedding. Helen immediately says 'I'm proud of you, Lil.' Lillian: 'Shut up, Helen!'
jokes.setup: Lillian has just done the most decisive thing she's done in the whole film — told Annie not to come to the wedding
jokes.punchline: Helen immediately tries to take credit for it; Lillian snaps at her too — revealing Helen's meddling has its own limits
jokes.explanation: Lillian's 'Shut up, Helen!' is a crowd-pleasing moment — it confirms that she still has some independence and that even she has limits with Helen's craving for validation. The beat is well-timed and character-specific.

jokes.text: In the aftermath of Annie's meltdown, Lillian asks if anyone else has anything to share. One guest raises her hand: 'I took two dogs already. They're in the back of my van.'
jokes.setup: Lillian asks 'Anybody else have anything they want to share?' — meaning emotional grievances
jokes.punchline: A guest sheepishly admits she's already stolen two party-favor dogs and they're in her van
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to the whole shower scene. After all the emotional chaos, one party guest has quietly been solving the dog-favor problem in the most practical and illegal way possible. 'They're in the back of my van' is a magnificent line — the specificity of 'the van' is what makes it land. Great economy, great timing, tremendous payoff on the dogs-as-party-favors gag. The delivery of complete matter-of-fact confession in the middle of emotional wreckage is exactly right.

jokes.text: Annie, while fleeing in her car, appears to cause a minor fender-bender — observed by Rhodes, who quips: 'Hit and run! Classy! Perfect! Okay.'
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to escape the shower in her already-broken car
jokes.punchline: She hits something on the way out; Rhodes, who had the voicemail callback earlier, witnesses it and delivers perfect deadpan commentary
jokes.explanation: Rhodes' commentary is funny and in character — he's a cop watching someone commit a minor traffic crime. 'Classy! Perfect! Okay.' is good deadpan. Sets up the taillight stop that follows.

jokes.text: Rhodes pulls Annie over: 'I can't say I'm surprised. I did tell you to get your lights fixed.' — 'Yeah, I know.' — 'And now here we are.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes pulls Annie over for the same broken taillights he's been warning her about throughout the film
jokes.punchline: 'And now here we are' — the gentlest, most resigned 'I told you so' in cinema
jokes.explanation: 'And now here we are' as a callback payoff is perfect — Rhodes isn't triumphant, just mildly weary. It's entirely in character: he's not punishing her, just noting the obvious. The comedy here comes from the understatement and from how much the taillights have been built up as a running gag.

jokes.text: Rhodes, breaking up with Annie, tells her: 'For the record, Annie, you flirted with me... and then you just left, just like it was nothing.'
jokes.setup: Annie attempts to end their conversation quickly; Rhodes stops her
jokes.punchline: Rhodes expresses legitimate hurt in a way that's almost comically earnest — his candidness about his own feelings in this precise, policeman way ('for the record') is both funny and unexpectedly touching
jokes.explanation: 'For the record' is a cop phrase repurposed for romantic hurt feelings — good character-specific comedy. The scene is more romantic drama than pure comedy but has genuine comedic texture.

jokes.text: Ted arrives — in uniform — after Annie apparently called him for roadside assistance: 'What's up, fuck-buddy? You call for some roadside assistance?'
jokes.setup: Annie, pulled over in an emotional moment with Rhodes, appears to have called someone else for help
jokes.punchline: Ted — her terrible casual sex partner — arrives in full police uniform, calling her 'fuck-buddy' in front of Rhodes
jokes.explanation: Ted arriving as the roadside assistance — and announcing himself as 'fuck-buddy' in front of the man Annie is falling for — is excellent comedic architecture. It's perfectly timed, creates maximum awkwardness, and Ted's oblivious enthusiasm is devastating. 'What's up, fuck-buddy' is quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: Annie's defense: 'I didn't have anyone else to call! I didn't know that you were gonna show up!' — Rhodes: 'That's the problem with cops, Annie. We're just never there when you need us.'
jokes.setup: Annie is mortified that Ted arrived in front of Rhodes; she tries to explain
jokes.punchline: Rhodes turns the moment into a cop joke — but delivered with enough bite that it's also genuinely sad
jokes.explanation: 'We're just never there when you need us' — a cop self-deprecating with a line that also registers as a real emotional wound. Good economy and character voice. The dual register (joke + hurt) is what makes Rhodes work as a character.

jokes.text: Ted drives off, says through the window: 'That cop talks weird.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes has just delivered an emotionally complex cop-metaphor breakup speech
jokes.punchline: Ted's takeaway is simply: 'That cop talks weird'
jokes.explanation: Four words that perfectly encapsulate Ted's character: he has absorbed nothing of emotional depth, only noting a surface oddity. 'That cop talks weird' is a great button — maximum economy, maximum character revelation. Ted consistently delivers laughs through his sheer obliviousness.

jokes.text: Ted drives Annie home: 'You know, you look tired. If you're tired, you can totally lay down in my lap, if you want.'
jokes.setup: Ted is driving Annie home; she's emotionally devastated
jokes.punchline: Ted offers a 'lap-nap' — framing an obvious come-on as genuine concern
jokes.explanation: The 'lap-nap' is a funny coinage, and Ted's oblivious sincerity in offering it is in character. 'Open for biz' as a follow-up is a nice touch — he's essentially advertising the lap. Solid character comedy, not exceptional.

jokes.text: Annie says she'd rather be murdered by the side of the road than spend another half-hour with Ted. Ted: 'Besides, I would never last a half-hour.'
jokes.setup: Annie says she'd rather get murdered than ride with Ted for another thirty minutes
jokes.punchline: Ted re-frames 'half-hour' as sexual duration — revealing himself incapable of non-sexual interpretation of anything
jokes.explanation: 'I would never last a half-hour' is a good line that works because Ted processes everything sexually and without shame. His self-deprecation is accidental. Good economy and character integration — only Ted says this.

jokes.text: Ted shouts at departing Annie: 'If you're trying to turn me on, it's working!' then 'You are no longer my number three!'
jokes.setup: Annie has gotten out of Ted's car in disgust
jokes.punchline: Ted's consolation prize of an insult — she's been demoted from his rotating hookup list
jokes.explanation: 'You are no longer my number three!' is an excellent character-specific line. Only Ted would (a) have a numbered list, (b) reveal its existence, and (c) think demotion from that list constitutes a meaningful punishment. The logic is completely within Ted's worldview. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Ted watches Annie walk away into the dark and calls after her: 'If you're trying to turn me on, it's working.'
jokes.setup: Annie has dramatically exited Ted's car into what she implied was murder territory
jokes.punchline: Ted reads her angry exit as sexual — a final button on his complete inability to read any situation correctly
jokes.explanation: Good character button. Ted interpreting literally everything as a come-on is consistent and funny. The line is delivered into the void as Annie walks away, which adds to the pathos-comedy of the moment.

jokes.text: Ted shouts after Annie: 'You used me! You are no longer my number three!'
jokes.setup: Annie has dismissed Ted; he has an emotional reaction to being 'used'
jokes.punchline: Ted's indignation at being 'used' is itself absurd given the nature of their relationship — but the revelation that Annie was 'number three' on a ranked list of casual partners is the genuine punchline
jokes.explanation: Excellent. The irony of Ted feeling 'used' is already funny given context, but 'you are no longer my number three' is the real joke — it reveals Ted maintains a ranked list of casual partners, Annie was number three (not even one or two), and being removed from the list is meant as punishment. All of this is implied in seven words. Very economical, very specific to Ted's character, and very quotable.

jokes.text: Megan has adopted nine dogs from the party and is struggling to manage them in Annie's mom's house
jokes.setup: Helen was giving away dogs as party favors; we know one guest took two already
jokes.punchline: Megan took NINE — and is regretting it, trying to herd them through the house
jokes.explanation: Megan taking nine dogs is the perfect Megan joke — she overcommits spectacularly, never does anything by halves. The visual of nine dogs being herded in the house is slapstick gold. The callback triple-layers the dog gag.

jokes.text: Megan confesses: 'I took nine. Yeah, I did slightly over-commit to the whole dog thing. It turns out I'm probably more comfortable with six.'
jokes.setup: Megan has nine dogs running loose in the house
jokes.punchline: 'I'm probably more comfortable with six' — delivered as a reasonable, considered adjustment, not an admission of catastrophic error
jokes.explanation: Megan's calibration of an acceptable number of impulsively stolen dogs is a perfect character moment. 'More comfortable with six' implies she regularly operates at a level that most people would find completely overwhelming — she's just adjusting her personal baseline. The understated delivery of a genuinely absurd self-assessment is Megan's comedic signature. High character integration: this line works because of everything we know about Megan.

jokes.text: Megan physically wrestles with Annie on the couch to get her to 'fight back': 'I'm life! I'm going to bite you in the ass!' — then slapping Annie repeatedly
jokes.setup: Megan is trying to motivate Annie with a tough-love speech
jokes.punchline: The 'speech' devolves into Megan physically attacking Annie while screaming 'I'm life!'
jokes.explanation: The idea that Megan's therapy is to physically embody 'life' and attack Annie is fully absurdist and completely character-specific — no one else in this movie does this. 'I'm life and I'm going to bite you in the ass' is a genuinely funny line. Megan's physical approach to emotional support is a perfect character expression.

jokes.text: Megan: 'Stop slapping yourself. Stop slapping yourself.' — Annie is being physically controlled into slapping herself
jokes.setup: Megan is physically wrestling with Annie on the couch in a 'motivational' session
jokes.punchline: The fight has devolved into the classic 'stop hitting yourself' playground move — Megan using Annie's own hand to slap her
jokes.explanation: The 'stop hitting yourself' move is a classic bit, so originality is docked. But in context — coming from Megan, in a motivational therapy session — it still lands. The absurdism of the situation carries it. Craft is average but impact is decent because of the physical performance.

jokes.text: Annie punches Megan in the face. Megan: 'Nice hit. All right. I'm glad to see you've got a little bit of spark in you. I knew that Annie was in there somewhere.'
jokes.setup: Megan is physically 'motivating' Annie; Annie has been passive
jokes.punchline: Annie finally hits back — and Megan's response is pure delight: 'Nice hit.' The violence was the goal all along
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Megan physical-therapy sequence. 'Nice hit' is perfect — Megan's immediate, genuine approval of being punched confirms that this whole scene was designed to get Annie to fight back. It works as both comedy and emotional beat. High character integration because this is exactly who Megan is.

jokes.text: Megan prefaces her inspirational story: 'I know you look at me now and think, "Boy, she must have breezed through high school."'
jokes.setup: Megan is about to share her inspirational backstory
jokes.punchline: The assumption that anyone would look at Megan — a bulky, eccentric government agent who just physically attacked her friend — and think she 'breezed through high school' is the joke
jokes.explanation: A great setup line. Megan's completely sincere confidence that she projects an image of social ease is funny precisely because she projects the opposite. The gap between her self-perception and reality is the entire Megan joke, and this line crystallizes it. 'Not the case, Annie' as a follow-up is perfectly dry.

jokes.text: Megan: 'They used to try to blow me up. They threw firecrackers at my head. I mean literally. I'm not saying that figuratively.'
jokes.setup: Megan is sharing her inspirational high school experience
jokes.punchline: The clarification — 'I mean literally. I'm not saying that figuratively' — takes what could be a hyperbolic expression and insists it was real, which makes it both darker and funnier
jokes.explanation: The clarification is what makes this line great. Without 'I mean literally,' it's a garden-variety 'I had it tough' story. With it, the joke pivots: Megan was literally targeted with explosives and she's presenting this as a motivational origin story. The dark specificity ('firecrackers at my head') and the earnest insistence on the literal reading are both very funny. High marks for structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Megan reveals she has the highest government security clearance, knows where all the nukes are and the launch codes — 'A lot of shopping malls. Don't repeat that!'
jokes.setup: Megan is explaining her success story: she turned her hard life around and 'works for the government'
jokes.punchline: She reveals classified nuclear information — specifically that nukes are hidden in shopping malls — and immediately panics
jokes.explanation: One of the best Megan jokes in the film. The absurdist escalation is perfect: her 'government job' keeps getting bigger (highest clearance, knows codes, knows locations) until she accidentally reveals actual classified information — and the specific detail 'a lot of shopping malls' is exactly the right level of mundane-surreal. The 'Don't repeat that!' after is a great button. This is the highest-scoring joke in this section of the film alongside the asshole joke, fully earned on originality, character specificity, and economy.

jokes.text: Megan: 'I have six houses. I bought an 18-wheeler a couple of months ago just because I could.'
jokes.setup: Megan is listing her achievements to inspire Annie
jokes.punchline: The 18-wheeler — bought purely as a power move — is an absurdly specific detail that reveals Megan's entire worldview
jokes.explanation: 'I bought an 18-wheeler just because I could' is excellent Megan characterization. The truck — not a yacht, not a mansion, an 18-wheeler — tells you everything. It's Megan's specific brand of imposing, utilitarian power fantasy. Great economy and character specificity.

jokes.text: Megan delivers her life philosophy: 'You're your problem, Annie. And you're also your solution.'
jokes.setup: Megan has been building to an inspirational climax
jokes.punchline: The wisdom lands — it's actually good advice — delivered by a woman who just physically attacked her friend and admitted to stealing nine dogs
jokes.explanation: The joke is partly structural: genuinely decent life advice delivered by the most chaotic person in the film. The line itself is good, the comedic value comes from the source. Good economy — it's pithy — but the content itself is a standard self-help aphorism, which keeps originality lower.

jokes.text: Megan's wisdom: 'You're your problem, Annie. And you're also your solution.'
jokes.setup: Megan has delivered an absurdist monologue and is arriving at the inspirational point
jokes.punchline: The 'wisdom' is genuine — it's actually sound life advice — but coming from someone who was just physically wrestling Annie and revealing nuclear codes, it lands as unexpectedly profound comedy
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the contrast — this is legitimately good advice delivered by someone who just confessed to knowing nuclear codes. The wisdom is real, which makes Megan more interesting as a character. Warm and funny.

jokes.text: Post-emotional hug, Megan says: 'Man, you have got to wash your hair.'
jokes.setup: Megan and Annie have just had a genuine emotional connection — a heartfelt hug
jokes.punchline: Megan, true to form, immediately follows the tender moment with a blunt hygiene critique
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the entire Megan scene. The emotional moment is genuine and the audience is invested — which makes the puncture of 'Man, you have got to wash your hair' even funnier. It's completely in character: Megan is supportive but also constitutionally incapable of letting a moment be purely sentimental. Maximum economy (seven words). The timing — mid-hug — is impeccable. This is a 'topper' that works because it doesn't deflate the emotion, it just adds Megan's specific flavor to it.

jokes.text: Annie is at a diner, discovers her car repairs are free: 'Rhodes and I worked out a deal way back when, so it's on the house.'
jokes.setup: Annie expects to pay for her car repairs after her disastrous day
jokes.punchline: Rhodes quietly arranged for them to be free — the taillights he kept nagging her about are finally fixed, at his expense, without announcement
jokes.explanation: A warm comedy beat that is primarily a character reveal about Rhodes — but it's also funny because the taillights gag has been built up so much that having them silently, generously fixed is the perfect anti-climax. The joke is in the understatement: the biggest running gag in the reel resolved by a mechanic saying 'it's on the house.'

jokes.text: Annie introduces her mom to someone at the diner. The person immediately says: 'Wait a minute, don't I know you from AA? Oh, my gosh. You made that artichoke dip, didn't you?'
jokes.setup: Annie is having a quiet diner moment with her mom — a brief respite after all the chaos
jokes.punchline: Her mom is immediately recognized from AA — with the specific detail of an artichoke dip, suggesting this person considers AA primarily a social eating event
jokes.explanation: The AA recognition is funny, but 'You made that artichoke dip!' elevates it. It transforms AA into a dinner party where someone became known for their dip rather than their sobriety struggle. It's a funny, specific detail that characterizes the mom and her social world without being mean-spirited. 'It's good, huh? It's just delicious' as a proud response is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Mom offers a tuna fish sandwich at 8am and suggests putting syrup on it
jokes.setup: Annie's mom offers to fix a tuna fish sandwich as comfort; Annie points out it's 8am
jokes.punchline: Mom's solution to the inappropriateness of the timing is to put syrup on it, as if that makes it a breakfast item
jokes.explanation: The joke works because the mom's logic is internally consistent in a completely unhinged way. She doesn't abandon the tuna fish idea; she adapts it. The syrup pivot is the punchline that reveals her character — well-meaning, slightly deranged, clueless. The economy is excellent: three lines, fully realized absurdist beat.

jokes.text: Helen tells Annie 'You should know, right? You're her best friend. It's weird that you don't know.'
jokes.setup: Helen is ostensibly apologizing and asking for help finding Lillian
jokes.punchline: She can't resist twisting the knife — implying it's Annie's fault for not knowing where the missing bride is
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the character: Helen is trying to be cooperative but passive aggression is so hardwired into her that she can't help herself. The double-down 'You guys are so close' adds a beat that lets the audience sit with the insult. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Helen pivots from apology to 'Harry never really wants to talk to me, either. He travels a lot. Like, all year. I'm basically just by myself.'
jokes.setup: Annie refuses to hear Helen's apology; Helen says 'I don't want to hear any more, honestly'
jokes.punchline: Helen immediately makes it about herself and her lonely marriage, forcing Annie into an awkward position of having to respond to this unexpected overshare
jokes.explanation: This is a great character joke. Helen's perfect life is revealed to be hollow in real time, and she does it in the most socially tone-deaf way possible. Annie's refusal — 'I don't feel sorry for you' — is the sharp button. The joke recontextualizes Helen without excusing her, which is sophisticated writing.

jokes.text: Helen says 'I think people just ask me to their weddings because I'm good at organizing parties. I don't have any female friends.'
jokes.setup: Helen is opening up about her emotional inadequacy; the conversation has turned genuine
jokes.punchline: The blunt self-assessment — delivered with almost clinical remove — is both sad and funny. The irony is that she's gained self-awareness too late and in the wrong way.
jokes.explanation: The humor comes from the gap between Helen's social ambition and her actual social reality. The two-sentence confession is devastatingly economical. It's also a callback payoff to everything we've learned about Helen — the competitive friendship hijacking, the performative generosity. All of that suddenly has a sad explanation, which makes it funnier and more poignant simultaneously.

jokes.text: Annie tells crying Helen: 'It's just the first time I've ever seen you look ugly. And that makes me kind of happy.'
jokes.setup: Helen asks why Annie is smiling during their emotional reconciliation moment
jokes.punchline: Annie confesses with barely concealed glee that Helen's ugly crying is the first time she's ever looked less than perfect, and it brings Annie genuine joy
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the reel and one of the film's finest. It's funny, honest, and character-perfect. Annie doesn't pretend to have risen above her jealousy — she admits it with a smile, and it's completely relatable. The structure is perfect: the setup is a moment of emotional vulnerability, the punchline is gleeful cattiness, and the extended back-and-forth ('I look ugly? No I don't') adds escalating comedy as Helen, even in breakdown, can't accept it. Scores 8+ because it's character-integrated in a way very few jokes achieve — only THIS character, in THIS relationship, at THIS moment could land this line.

jokes.text: Helen insists 'I'm not really an ugly crier' and 'But I still look pretty good' while visibly falling apart
jokes.setup: Annie has just told Helen she's an ugly crier and Helen is trying to dispute it
jokes.punchline: Even at her lowest emotional point, Helen cannot surrender her self-image; she pivots from denial to rationalizing ('it's just my makeup') to a defiant 'I still look pretty good'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Helen's denial — from 'no I don't' to 'maybe just a little' negotiated down to 'it's just my makeup' to the triumphant 'but I still look pretty good' — is a small masterpiece of character comedy. It's entirely earned by everything we know about Helen and lands harder because it comes in the middle of a genuine emotional scene.

jokes.text: Annie hangs out the car window screaming 'Rhodes! Rhodes! Come on! Rhodes!' while Officer Rhodes visibly ignores her
jokes.setup: Annie needs Rhodes' help but he is driving past ignoring her; she and Helen are in a moving car
jokes.punchline: The desperation of Annie hanging out of a car window screaming a cop's name in traffic is pure physical comedy; Helen offering to take over ('He's ignoring you. Let me.') adds a layer
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy setup. The joke is in Annie's desperation and the irony of needing to flag down a cop who is actively ignoring her. Helen's calm takeover attempt is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Annie driving recklessly — swerving, throwing litter out the window — to get a cop's attention, while Helen screams 'Annie, my hair! What are you doing?'
jokes.setup: Annie needs to get Officer Rhodes to pull her over so she can talk to him
jokes.punchline: She commits increasingly absurd traffic violations — reckless driving, littering, 'Here comes the litter-bug!' — with Helen's vanity-focused panic ('Annie, my hair!') as counterpoint
jokes.explanation: The escalating traffic violations work as a comedic set piece. 'Here comes the litter-bug!' delivered with performative relish is a highlight. Helen complaining about her hair while Annie commits traffic violations is a perfect character contrast — each reacting in completely in-character ways to chaos.

jokes.text: 'Let's see what Marmaduke's doing. Just texting. Talking on the phone while I'm driving. Not even using my hands.'
jokes.setup: Annie is cataloguing her traffic violations to try to get pulled over
jokes.punchline: She narrates her own violations like a nature documentary, naming Rhodes 'Marmaduke' and proudly announcing each infraction with gleeful commentary
jokes.explanation: The 'Marmaduke' nickname is an unexpected absurdist detail that elevates what could be generic physical comedy. Annie's cheerful self-narration of her own crimes has a manic energy that is distinctly Wiig-as-Annie. The 'not even using my hands' escalation lands well.

jokes.text: Annie opens a beer and dramatically drinks it while driving: 'Mmm! Yum! Yum! Beer! Yum! Yum! Yum!'
jokes.setup: Annie is continuing to escalate her traffic violations to get pulled over
jokes.punchline: The theatrical, performative sipping — 'Mmm! Yum! Yum! Beer!' — is so over-the-top that it circles back from desperation to absurdism; Helen's flat 'Idiot' punctuates it perfectly
jokes.explanation: The 'Yum! Yum! Beer!' delivery is peak Wiig absurdism — a character performing for an audience of one who isn't watching. Helen's one-word verdict 'Idiot' is a perfectly dry button.

jokes.text: Helen screaming 'I'm going to hurl. I feel really sick, Annie!' from the passenger seat
jokes.setup: Annie has been driving recklessly through all of this
jokes.punchline: Helen — the composed, perfect woman — is about to vomit. Her distress is entirely Annie-caused, and her phrasing ('I'm going to hurl') is incongruously casual for someone so refined
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat. Helen saying 'hurl' rather than something more dignified is a small character joke. Not the strongest moment in the sequence but contributes to the escalation.

jokes.text: Annie announces 'I'm topless! I'm totally topless.' to get Rhodes' attention
jokes.setup: Annie has exhausted conventional traffic violations and is running out of ideas
jokes.punchline: She goes nuclear with a topless announcement; Rhodes' 'Really?' followed by 'Wow. Unbelievable.' suggests he looked — and what he saw did not deliver on the promise
jokes.explanation: The joke has a classic misdirection structure: 'I'm topless' promises something titillating, Rhodes' 'Really?' suggests he looked, and 'Wow. Unbelievable.' — combined with 'What the fuck are you doing?' — reframes it as a reaction to chaos, not attraction. The beat works in the escalating sequence.

jokes.text: Rhodes: 'All of that stuff, that would have been dangerous for a good driver.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes confronts Annie after she's committed a litany of traffic violations to get his attention
jokes.punchline: His critique is not of the violations themselves but of her driving ability — an absurd hierarchy of concerns that sidesteps the insanity entirely
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. The joke is perfectly constructed: the expected response to Annie's chaos is anger or disbelief; instead Rhodes delivers a measured, almost bureaucratic critique of her driving competence, entirely bypassing the insanity. The deadpan condescension reveals his character while getting a huge laugh. 'For a good driver' is the key phrase — the implication being that she is not one. Economically perfect, highly quotable, completely character-specific.

jokes.text: Rhodes pulls them over: 'What the fuck are you doing?' Annie: 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes has finally stopped after Annie's escalating violations; he's furious
jokes.punchline: Annie's completely honest, resigned 'I don't know' — no defense, no excuse — is perfect deflation after all the escalation
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the set piece. The two-word punchline 'I don't know' earns maximum points for economy — it's the most honest thing Annie could say and completely collapses the tension of the chase in one beat. The exhaustion in the delivery is essential. This is excellent comic structure.

jokes.text: Helen introduces herself to Rhodes: 'This is Helen. I'm Helen.' — Rhodes responds warmly 'Hello, Helen. I've heard wonderful things.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes asks who the other woman in the car is
jokes.punchline: Rhodes claims to have 'heard wonderful things' about Helen — given that Annie has been his source, this is impossible and vaguely sycophantic in a way that gently mocks him
jokes.explanation: A quiet joke. The irony of Rhodes having 'heard wonderful things' about the woman Annie has been complaining about is understated. It works more as a character beat for Rhodes — slightly awkward, trying to be polite — than as a big laugh.

jokes.text: Rhodes: 'It's this kind of high-octane stuff that really made me want to become a cop. Missing girl found at her apartment. It's adrenalin-pinching.'
jokes.setup: Lillian has been found at her own apartment — where they already looked — making the whole panic pointless
jokes.punchline: Rhodes delivers a mock-heroic eulogy for the non-crisis, inventing the word 'adrenalin-pinching' (rather than 'pumping') as a deflating synonym
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. 'Adrenalin-pinching' is a perfect original coinage — it inverts the cliché 'adrenalin-pumping' into something much smaller and more pathetic, perfectly capturing the anticlimax. The whole speech ('this kind of high-octane stuff...') is a dry, beautifully constructed bit of deadpan. Character-specific: Rhodes is earnest, slightly square, and finds dignity in small-scale police work. The joke is entirely earned and genuinely quotable.

jokes.text: Rhodes: 'I'm glad that you got your taillights fixed. Means I won't have to stop you again.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes and Annie part ways after the crisis is resolved; there is unresolved romantic tension
jokes.punchline: Instead of a romantic goodbye, Rhodes makes a callback to the traffic stop that began their relationship — suggesting their connection will end now that the bureaucratic pretext is gone
jokes.explanation: A bittersweet callback that works both as a joke and as emotional punctuation. The understatement is the joke — Rhodes deflecting with mundane cop-talk instead of saying what he means. It's character-perfect and lands with the audience because we know the history.

jokes.text: Lillian: 'Yeah, wasn't it my turn to be crazy? The bride's supposed to be crazy.' Annie: 'You kind of stole all the crazy. I out-crazied you.'
jokes.setup: Annie and Lillian are reconciling; Annie acknowledges her behavior has been erratic throughout the wedding planning
jokes.punchline: 'I out-crazied you' — a tidy, self-aware summary of the entire film's premise, delivered with rueful affection
jokes.explanation: 'I out-crazied you' is a great line — compact, honest, and funny because it's both an apology and a brag. 'You kind of stole all the crazy' is the setup that makes it land. The exchange has genuine warmth without sacrificing the comedy.

jokes.text: Lillian in her wedding dress — visual gag of the dress being so enormous/unwearable that Annie's reaction ('Don't you dare laugh') implies it's a disaster
jokes.setup: Annie tells Lillian to get her dress on so they can go to the wedding; Lillian says 'That's the other problem'
jokes.punchline: Whatever Lillian looks like in the dress is so bad that Annie's first instinct is to warn herself not to laugh — the dress (presumably a Helen-designed over-the-top creation) has gone badly wrong
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in what we don't see (this being a transcript). 'Don't you dare laugh' tells the audience everything — whatever the dress looks like is bad enough that Annie's first reflex is to suppress her own laughter. Then 'I cannot wear this dress!' confirms it. The setup-to-visual-reveal structure is a classic comedy construction.

jokes.text: Lillian: 'Do you have a chainsaw and a blowtorch?'
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to calm Lillian down about the dress disaster, saying 'We'll fix it. We'll tweak it.'
jokes.punchline: Lillian's response implies the dress is so catastrophically bad that the only solutions are tools of destruction, not fashion
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that demolish Annie's optimism and convey the full scale of the dress disaster. The specificity of 'chainsaw AND blowtorch' (two tools, neither of which is a sewing implement) is what makes it funny rather than just hyperbolic. Highly quotable and structurally airtight.

jokes.text: Annie: 'If Helen had anything to do with this wedding, it is going to be perfect and tasteful and beautiful.' — played as genuine reassurance that is also a backhand to Annie's own efforts
jokes.setup: Lillian worries the wedding will be a disaster; Annie tries to reassure her
jokes.punchline: Annie's reassurance is premised entirely on Helen's competence — which implicitly acknowledges that Annie herself has been the source of disasters throughout the film
jokes.explanation: A bittersweet joke with real character depth. Annie is genuinely trying to be kind, and in doing so, she admits that her rival is better at this than she is. 'Perfect and tasteful and beautiful' — three words that could describe Helen and implicitly don't describe Annie's contributions. The joke only works because we know the full history.

jokes.text: Helen's father: 'I am not paying for this shit.' — whispered reaction to Wilson Phillips performing at the wedding reception
jokes.setup: The MC announces that Wilson Phillips — Lillian's favorite band — is here to perform live at the reception
jokes.punchline: An older man's flat, appalled financial objection cuts through the joy of the moment
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Wilson Phillips as surprise wedding entertainment is itself absurd, and the man's response is the perfectly pragmatic, non-sentimental counterpoint to everyone else's joy. 'I am not paying for this shit' is economically perfect — six words that say everything. The understated delivery (presumably muttered) makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Helen to Lillian's father: 'It's the last one, I promise. The last one. The last one.' — reassuring him about the wedding expenses
jokes.setup: Lillian's father is appalled at the cost of booking Wilson Phillips
jokes.punchline: Helen's triple 'the last one' — said with the cadence of someone who has said this many times — implies this is not, in fact, the last expensive thing she has done
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'the last one' has the quality of a person who has had this conversation before and knows it isn't true. Good character moment — Helen's compulsive one-upmanship is apparently applied even to wedding expenses.

jokes.text: During Wilson Phillips' performance, Megan leans to Annie and whispers: 'I put a loaded gun in Dougie's carry-on. The TSA is going to just rip his ass apart.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is watching Wilson Phillips perform at the wedding reception in a warm, emotional moment
jokes.punchline: Megan, mid-song, casually reveals she has committed what is essentially a federal crime as a prank on the groom — delivered with complete satisfaction
jokes.explanation: The best joke in this reel by a significant margin. The timing — whispered during a tender moment in a love song — is perfect. The content is completely unexpected and maximally Megan: she has weaponized the honeymoon to terrorize the groom with TSA, apparently out of pure chaotic loyalty to Lillian. 'The TSA is going to just rip his ass apart' is the punchline — specific, vivid, and delivered with cheerful anticipation. This is exactly the kind of joke that becomes a cultural touchstone: shocking, perfectly in-character, and utterly original. High quotability, memorable, and earns every point. Comparable to the vasectomy anchor example in character specificity and shock value.

jokes.text: Annie tells Helen 'it was really nice meeting you' — a formal goodbye to someone she has known for months through intense shared experiences
jokes.setup: Annie and Helen have their final scene together after the wedding
jokes.punchline: Using first-meeting social niceties for someone you've had a full emotional arc with — including fighting, reconciling, and crying together — is an absurd deflation of everything that came before
jokes.explanation: A quiet, earned joke. The formality is the joke — both characters retreating to social convention rather than the messy reality of what they've been through. It's character-consistent for Annie (awkward, conflict-avoidant) and Helen (performatively polite).

jokes.text: Annie invites Helen to 'Rockin' Sushi' — the restaurant from an earlier disaster — as an olive branch
jokes.setup: Annie is extending an olive branch to Helen as they part ways after the wedding
jokes.punchline: She chooses 'Rockin' Sushi' — almost certainly a reference to a terrible restaurant from their shared past — as the venue for future friendship. Helen accepts.
jokes.explanation: A callback that doubles as a character moment — Annie offering the specific site of an earlier conflict as a future meeting place is either oblivious or deliberately ironic. Helen's acceptance suggests genuine goodwill. Works as a character beat more than a big laugh.

jokes.text: Rhodes: 'I ate your cake that you left. I had to fight some raccoons off. But that's okay. I'm pretty strong and tough, so it wasn't much of a contest.'
jokes.setup: Rhodes has shown up to give Annie a ride; this is their reunion after their falling-out
jokes.punchline: Instead of a romantic declaration, he leads with eating her abandoned cake and casually asserting his physical dominance over raccoons as if this is unremarkable
jokes.explanation: Rhodes' delivery of this information is perfectly in character — he's affectionate but channeling everything through mundane cop-adjacent competence claims. 'I'm pretty strong and tough, so it wasn't much of a contest' is the killer line: a grown man seriously asserting raccoon-fighting ability as a romantic credential. The specificity and earnestness of it is what makes it work.

jokes.text: Annie cuts off Rhodes mid-sentence: 'I'm just going to kiss you now rather than just...'
jokes.setup: Rhodes is about to say something; Annie is in a romantic moment and starts to explain herself
jokes.punchline: She interrupts herself — and presumably him — by just going in for the kiss rather than completing the sentence, which is the most Annie possible response
jokes.explanation: A cute character moment. The incomplete sentence is funny because it's relatable — sometimes you just stop talking and do the thing. Annie's particular brand of social awkwardness makes the truncated declaration feel true to character.

jokes.text: Rhodes: 'Oh! I'm on duty. And I need to put my uniform on. If I drive like this, they're gonna think I just stole a car, which wouldn't be great.'
jokes.setup: Annie and Rhodes are kissing; Rhodes breaks away because his radio has gone off
jokes.punchline: His response to the romantic moment is entirely practical and mildly absurd — the concern about looking like a car thief rather than focusing on the kiss is classic Rhodes deadpan
jokes.explanation: Rhodes' priorities — duty first, appearances second, romance last — are consistent character comedy. 'Which wouldn't be great' is a lovely understatement button.

jokes.text: Rhodes forces Annie to sit in the back seat of his police car: 'You can't sit in the front, it's against regulations.'
jokes.setup: Annie is invited to ride along with Rhodes; she moves to get in the front
jokes.punchline: He makes his romantic interest sit in the prisoner section of a police car because rules are rules
jokes.explanation: Perfect character joke for Rhodes — he is so procedurally correct that he won't bend even for someone he's romantically interested in. The visual of Annie being relegated to the back of a cop car on a date is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Rhodes: 'Sorry. Habit. It's a force of habit.' — after making Annie get in the back of the cop car
jokes.setup: Annie protests being put in the back seat
jokes.punchline: Rhodes' explanation — that putting people in the back is simply habit — implies he does this so often that he did it on autopilot even with a date. The double understatement ('Sorry. Habit. It's a force of habit.') is a small gem.
jokes.explanation: The joke in 'habit' is that it reveals Rhodes has arrested so many people that putting a passenger in the back is automatic. The triple restatement — 'Sorry. Habit. It's a force of habit.' — has a rhythm that plays as nervous justification, which is funny.

jokes.text: Rhodes reveals there is 'a warrant out for Annie's arrest' — listing all the traffic violations she committed to get his attention
jokes.setup: Annie asks to be moved to the front seat; Rhodes says there's a warrant for her arrest
jokes.punchline: He lists: 'Reckless driving, littering, texting, consuming alcohol while operating a vehicle' — all the violations she performed for him — and 'You didn't think I was going to let you get away with that, did you?'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured callback. The audience has forgotten that Annie actually committed real crimes; Rhodes' list reminds us that everything she did was genuine and prosecutable. 'You didn't think I was going to let you get away with that, did you?' is the perfect button — it's both romantic (he noticed her) and cop-ish (he will not be overlooking crimes). The structure pays off the earlier set piece in a completely satisfying way.

jokes.text: Annie, sitting in the back of a police car under arrest, asks: 'Could we put the siren on? Please?'
jokes.setup: Annie has just been informed she is under arrest and is in the back seat
jokes.punchline: Her response to being arrested is not protest but a request to enjoy the police car experience — childlike delight displacing any rational concern
jokes.explanation: One of the best character jokes in the reel. Annie's psychological journey has been downward — she's been arrested, is in a police car, her best friend just got married — and her response is pure childlike wonder about the siren. It's perfectly Annie: she can't maintain an adult emotional register. The 'Please?' with its implication that she might actually get it is delightful. Very economical and quotable.

jokes.text: Post-credits: 'This is Tape 119. Air Marshall Jon and I's first sexual encounter.' — followed by absurdist bear-and-sandwich roleplay
jokes.setup: Post-credits scene: Megan announces this is a sex tape, Tape 119
jokes.punchline: The number '119' implies this is not unusual behavior for Megan; followed by her and Air Marshall Jon doing a bizarre 'hungry bear' and 'bear sandwich' roleplay with extremely committed delivery
jokes.explanation: The 'Tape 119' detail is the best gag in the sequence — the implication that Megan has 118 previous tapes recontextualizes her as someone who has been doing elaborate sexual cosplay for a very long time. The bear/sandwich roleplay is committed enough to be funny in its specificity. 'Is there a hungry bear anywhere?' with Jon's 'I'm a hungry bear' has an earnestness that sells the absurdism. 'Ham nipple' is a genuinely unexpected phrase that earns a reaction.

jokes.text: 'Fuck it up. I'm gonna fuck you up, ham nipple. Ham nipple. Fuck it up. A little hard. Ow! A little hard. A little hard.'
jokes.setup: The bear/sandwich roleplay continues to escalate
jokes.punchline: 'Ham nipple' as a term of... endearment? Aggression? The ambiguity and the 'ow' suggesting someone got actually hurt is the final escalating beat
jokes.explanation: 'Ham nipple' is unexpected enough to function as a genuine laugh line. The 'A little hard. Ow!' suggests the roleplay has gotten physically out of hand, which is a satisfying final escalation. The absurdism is fully committed to, which is what makes it land rather than just being random.

jokes.text: 'Hey, guess what. Guess what, ham. Fuck it up. I'm gonna fuck you up, ham nipple. Ham nipple. Fuck it up. A little hard. Ow! A little hard.'
jokes.setup: The bear/sandwich roleplay is in full swing
jokes.punchline: 'Ham nipple' — a word that should not exist but sounds exactly right for Megan to have invented in the heat of the moment; the escalation into physical comedy ('a little hard. Ow!') adds another layer
jokes.explanation: 'Ham nipple' is an invented compound noun that is both disgusting and extremely funny — it passes the test of being a word that does not exist but is exactly the right word for this moment. The scene escalates to physical discomfort ('Ow! A little hard') which grounds the absurdity in physical reality and gets a final laugh. Highly quotable by the standards of absurdist comedy.
